t: From Source Code to Production: The Whole Picture
x: Most developers learn programming from the inside out: a function, then a module, then an application that runs on their laptop. "Deployment" arrives later as a mysterious step where the application is "put on a server" and, hopefully, keeps working. That gap is where most production incidents, security breaches and budget overruns live. The code was fine. What failed was the certificate that expired, the database connection pool that was exhausted, the environment variable that was missing in staging but present in production, the S3 bucket that was public, the deploy that ran a migration before the old code had stopped using the column. This book is about everything that happens around and after the code. This first chapter gives you the whole map so that each subsequent chapter has a place to live.

x: "If it works on my machine and passes tests, it is done." Tests prove the code does what you think in the environment you tested. Production adds concurrency, hostile input, network failure, expiry, partial deploys and other people's changes. "The cloud handles reliability for me." AWS keeps its services running; you are responsible for running yours across Availability Zones, backing up your data, and configuring security. This is the shared responsibility model. "Security is a feature we add at the end." A system designed without trust boundaries cannot have them bolted on. The cheapest security work is done in design, the most expensive after a breach. "Kubernetes is how serious systems are deployed." Many serious, profitable systems run on a handful of containers on a managed service, or even on two well-configured virtual machines. Complexity is a cost paid every day; buy it only when the problem demands it. "Monitoring means a dashboard." A dashboard nobody is watching at 3 a.m. is decoration. Monitoring means alerts that page a human when users are affected, and the observability to find out why.

h: The problem: "run the code" is not one thing
x: When you type python app.py or node server.js , something turns text into CPU instructions. How that happens decides your start-up time, memory footprint, CPU efficiency, how many concurrent requests one process can handle, how you package and deploy it, and how you debug it when it is slow. Engineers who treat the runtime as a black box make predictable mistakes: they run one Python process on an 8-core machine and wonder why 7 cores idle; they block the Node event loop with a synchronous call and the whole server freezes; they ship a Go binary with no way to see what it is doing.

h: Three ways to execute source code

x: A compiler translates source into machine code for a specific CPU architecture and operating system before the program runs. Go, Rust, C and C++ work this way. The output is a binary: a file the kernel can load and jump into directly. Consequences for production: - Deployment is a file copy. A statically linked Go binary has no runtime dependencies. Container images can be built FROM scratch and weigh a few megabytes. - Start-up is instantaneous , which matters for autoscaling and serverless cold starts. - Cross-compilation is required : a binary built on an Apple Silicon laptop (arm64, macOS) will not run on an x86-64 Linux server. CI builds for the target platform. - Errors like type mismatches are caught at build time rather than at 3 a.m.

An interpreter reads the source (or a lightly processed form of it) and executes it step by step. CPython, the standard Python implementation, compiles each module to bytecode ( .pyc files in pycache ) and then runs that bytecode on a virtual machine written in C. Ruby and PHP behave similarly. Consequences: - The runtime must be installed on the server , at a compatible version, together with every dependency. This is why Python deployments historically broke so often and why containers became popular. - Start-up involves importing modules , which can take seconds for large applications. - Execution is slower per instruction than native code, often by an order of magnitude for pure-Python loops. Real applications spend most time in I/O or in C extensions (database drivers, JSON parsing, NumPy), so the gap matters less than benchmarks suggest. - Many errors surface only when the line executes. Type checkers like mypy and Pyright recover some compile-time safety.

A JIT runtime starts by interpreting and compiles hot code paths to machine code while the program runs, using observed types and branches to optimise. The JVM (Java, Kotlin), V8 (Node.js, browsers) and .NET work this way. Consequences: - Warm-up : the first few thousand requests are slower than steady state. Load tests and health checks must account for this; a JVM service can take 30 to 90 seconds to reach full speed. - Memory : JIT runtimes hold compiled code, profiling data and large heaps. A trivial Java service may need 256 MB; the JVM's default heap sizing inside containers has caused countless out-of-memory kills, discussed in chapter 7. - Peak performance can approach native code. title Execution models compared columns Property Ahead-of-time (Go, Rust) Interpreted (CPython) JIT (JVM, V8) Deploy artifact single binary source + runtime + deps bytecode/source + runtime Cold start milliseconds hundreds of ms to seconds seconds, plus warm-up Memory baseline very low low to moderate moderate to high Throughput per core lower (C extensions help) high after warm-up Error detection compile time run time (type checker helps) mixed Operational gotchas cross-compiling, no REPL GIL, dependency hell heap sizing, warm-up, GC pauses

h: What a runtime does for you
x: Whichever model, your code runs inside a runtime : the standard library plus machinery for memory management, concurrency and interaction with the operating system. Memory management. Go, Java, Python and JavaScript all use garbage collection: the runtime tracks which objects are still reachable and frees the rest. You do not call free() , but you pay in CPU time and, with some collectors, in pauses. A service that allocates heavily can show periodic latency spikes exactly when the collector runs. Rust and C make you manage memory explicitly, trading ergonomics for predictability. Concurrency. This is where runtimes differ most and where production behaviour is decided. - CPython and the GIL. The Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time within a process. Threads still help when work is I/O-bound (the lock is released while waiting on a socket), but CPU-bound work does not parallelise across threads. To use multiple cores you run multiple processes , which is why production Python servers (Gunicorn, uWSGI) fork workers. Recent Python versions have an optional free-threaded build, but as of late 2026 most production deployments still use the GIL build and the multi-process model. - asyncio (Python) and the event loop (Node.js). A single thread runs many tasks cooperatively; each yields when it awaits I/O. Extremely efficient for thousands of concurrent connections that are mostly waiting. h: Processes: how the operating system sees your service
x: The kernel does not know about Python or Node. It knows processes : an address space, a set of open file descriptors, environment variables, a user ID, a current directory and one or more threads scheduled onto CPUs. When you run a server, you are asking the kernel to create a process, load the runtime binary into it, and let the runtime load your code. Everything about deployment is ultimately about processes: - A container is a process with isolation applied (Part VI). - A systemd service is a process the init system starts, supervises and restarts (Part V). - A deploy stops old processes and starts new ones; a graceful shutdown means the process finishes in-flight requests after receiving SIGTERM before exiting (chapter 6). - A crash is a process exiting unexpectedly; the supervisor's job is to notice and restart it, and yours is to find out why from the logs.

h: Practical: running a FastAPI app in production
x: Development uses the auto-reloading single process: uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 Production uses a process manager with multiple workers, no reload, and binding to all interfaces inside the container: gunicorn app.main:app \ --worker-class uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker \ --workers 4 \ --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 \ --timeout 30 \ --graceful-timeout 20 \ --max-requests 5000 --max-requests-jitter 500 \ --access-logfile - --error-logfile - Each flag encodes a production lesson: Flag Lesson --- --- --workers 4 Use the cores. Start with 1 async worker per core, then load test. --timeout 30 A worker stuck for 30 seconds is killed and replaced; a hung request cannot wedge the server forever. Must exceed your slowest legitimate request. --graceful-timeout 20 On SIGTERM, workers get 20 seconds to finish current requests. Must be below the orchestrator's kill deadline (ECS default 30 s, Kubernetes default 30 s). --max-requests with jitter Recycles workers periodically to bound memory leaks; jitter stops all workers restarting at once. Logs to stdout/stderr The container runtime or systemd collects them. Never write log files inside containers. The Node.js equivalent is running one process per core with the cluster module or, more commonly, running one Node process per container and letting the orchestrator run several containers. Node's event loop handles concurrency within each process; CPU-bound work goes to worker threads or a separate service.

- Serverless cold starts are a direct consequence of runtime choice: a Go or Rust Lambda starts in tens of milliseconds, Python in a few hundred, a JVM in seconds without special tooling (SnapStart or GraalVM native images). - Right-sizing containers depends on the runtime's memory model. A Node service usually fits in 256 to 512 MB; a Spring Boot service wants 1 GB or more. Guessing wrong means OOM kills. - Polyglot teams standardise on a base image per runtime with the version pinned ( python:3.12-slim , node:22-alpine ), because "it worked locally on Python 3.11" is a real incident class.

- Runtimes have vulnerabilities. Patch them like any dependency: a Node or Python base image from a year ago carries known CVEs. - Interpreted languages make eval -style code execution easy; never pass untrusted input to eval , exec , pickle.loads or template engines without sandboxing (Part IV). - Debug servers ( --reload , Werkzeug debugger, Node --inspect bound to 0.0.0.0) must never run in production. The Werkzeug debugger allows arbitrary code execution to anyone who reaches it. - Expose runtime metrics: GC pauses, event loop lag, worker count, heap size. They explain latency spikes that application metrics cannot.

1. One process on a multi-core machine for a Python or Node service. Cores sit idle; throughput is a quarter of what you paid for. 2. Blocking the event loop with synchronous file or network calls, CPU-heavy loops, or a synchronous database driver in an async framework. h: The problem the operating system solves
x: A computer has a handful of CPUs, some memory, disks and network cards. Dozens or thousands of programs want to use them at the same time, written by people who do not trust each other, with bugs that would otherwise take the machine down. The operating system is the arbitration layer: it gives each program the illusion of its own machine, shares the real hardware fairly, enforces boundaries between programs, and offers a stable interface so programs do not need to know which brand of network card is installed. Every server-side problem that is not a logic bug in your code is, in some way, an operating system problem: the disk is full, the process ran out of file descriptors, the kernel killed something for memory, the TCP backlog overflowed, the clock drifted, a permission was denied. Learning the OS is learning to read those symptoms.

The kernel is the privileged core that talks to hardware. Your programs run in user space with restricted privileges. A user-space program cannot touch hardware, other processes' memory or the kernel's memory directly. When it needs something, it makes a system call: a controlled transition into the kernel to request a service such as "open this file", "send these bytes on this socket" or "give me more memory". title From your function call to the hardware layers Your code summary `requests.get(url)` or `fetch(url)`. Language runtime and libraries summary HTTP library builds the request, the runtime's socket module prepares a `send()`. Still user space. The runtime may add its own buffering and connection pooling. C library (libc) glibc / musl summary Wraps system calls in functions such as `write()`, `connect()`, `malloc()`. Alpine Linux uses musl rather than glibc, which is why some Python wheels fail on Alpine images. System call boundary summary CPU switches to privileged mode; the kernel validates arguments. Each transition costs roughly a microsecond. Programs that make millions of tiny system calls (unbuffered writes) are slow for this reason. `strace` shows them. Kernel subsystems scheduler, VFS, network stack, memory manager summary The kernel queues the bytes in a socket buffer, segments them into TCP packets, chooses a route. Tunable via sysctl: TCP buffer sizes, backlog length, file limits, swappiness. Device drivers summary Translate generic requests into command

A server with 4 cores and 300 runnable threads needs to decide who runs. The scheduler gives each runnable thread a short time slice (milliseconds), switches between them (a context switch ), and prioritises according to niceness and scheduling class. Threads waiting for I/O are not runnable and cost nothing until data arrives. What this means for you: - Load average (shown by uptime , top ) is the average number of threads that are running or waiting to run (and on Linux, also those in uninterruptible disk wait) over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load of 4 on a 4-core machine means the CPUs are fully busy; a load of 12 means threads are queueing three deep. Load above core count with low CPU utilisation points at I/O wait, not CPU. - Context switches are not free. Thousands of threads thrashing between each other spend their time in the scheduler rather than working. This is why event loops and goroutines exist: many logical tasks on few OS threads. - CPU steal ( st in top ) on a virtual machine is time the hypervisor gave to someone else. Burstable instances (AWS t3 ) show this when credits run out. # Snapshot of CPU, run queue (r), blocked (b), context switches (cs), wait (wa), steal (st) vmstat 1 5 # procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu----- # r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa st # 9 0 0 412340 102400 3981200 0 0 0 48 2311 9876 71 12 15 2 0 Reading that line: 9 runnable threads on (say) 4 cores, 71% user CPU, 12% system

Each process sees a private, contiguous address space; the kernel maps pages of that space onto physical RAM (or disk, if swapping) on demand. Two consequences you will meet in production: 1. Memory numbers are confusing. "Virtual size" (VSZ) is address space reserved; "resident set size" (RSS) is physical memory actually in use; shared libraries are counted in several processes at once. Container memory limits apply to the cgroup's accounting, which includes page cache in some configurations. Chapter 7 untangles this. 2. The page cache. Linux uses free RAM to cache file contents. A server showing 95% memory "used" with most of it as cache is healthy; the cache is given back instantly when a process needs it. free -h shows this as buff/cache and available . Alerting on "used memory" without excluding cache causes false alarms. When memory truly runs out, the kernel invokes the oom killer, picking a process (usually the largest) and killing it. In a container, the whole container is killed with exit code 137.

Programs see files and directories; the Virtual File System (VFS) layer hides whether they are on an ext4 partition, an NFS share, a tmpfs in memory, or a FUSE mount. Important behaviours: - Everything is a file descriptor. Open files, sockets, pipes and devices all consume entries in a per-process table with a limit ( ulimit -n , commonly 1024 by default). A service that opens many connections or files without closing them hits "Too many open files" and starts failing in bizarre ways. Production services raise the limit (systemd LimitNOFILE=65536 ) and, more importantly, fix the leak. - Writes are buffered. write() returns when the kernel has the data, not when it is on disk. Durability requires fsync() , which databases call religiously and which is why database disk latency matters so much. - Deleting an open file does not free space. The directory entry disappears but the blocks remain until the last process closes it. Classic incident: disk 100% full, du finds nothing, because a rotated log file is still held open by a process. lsof +L1 finds the culprit. - Permissions are enforced here (chapter 5).

The kernel implements TCP, UDP and IP. Your program hands bytes to a socket; the kernel does segmentation, retransmission, congestion control and routing. Buffers sit between them: a send buffer per socket, a receive buffer per socket, and a listen backlog of connections that completed the handshake but have not yet been accept() ed by your program. The backlog matters for web servers: if your process is too slow to accept connections, the backlog fills, and new connections are dropped or get a reset. Nginx and Gunicorn set it explicitly, bounded by the kernel's net.core.somaxconn . Part II goes deep on all of this; for now, know that "connection refused" and "connection timed out" are OS-level messages with specific meanings.

Servers keep time with a system clock disciplined by NTP (chrony or systemd-timesyncd). Drift of even a minute breaks TLS certificate validation at the margins, AWS API request signing (which rejects requests more than 5 minutes off), JWT expiry checks, and log correlation across machines. Containers share the host clock. Always run time synchronisation; on EC2 use the Amazon Time Sync Service at 169.254.169.123 . Related: store and transmit timestamps in UTC; convert to local time only for display. Timezone bugs are a steady source of incidents that appear exactly twice a year.

The kernel enforces that a process running as user app cannot read files owned by root with mode 600, cannot bind ports below 1024 without a capability, cannot send signals to other users' processes, and cannot load kernel modules. Running services as root throws this protection away: a vulnerability in the application becomes a compromise of the machine. Chapter 5 and Part V cover users and permissions; Part VI covers the namespaces and cgroups that containers add on top.

A typical investigation of "the API is slow" on a Linux host goes through the OS layers in order: 1. uptime and top : is the CPU saturated? Load vs cores? Steal? 2. free -h and dmesg grep -i oom : memory pressure? OOM kills? 3. df -h and df -i : disk or inodes full? 4. iostat -x 1 : disk latency ( await ) and utilisation? 5. ss -s and ss -ltnp : socket counts, listening ports, backlog overflow? 6. journalctl -u myapp -n 200 : what did the service itself say? Several programs share one machine: the web server, your application, a database, a backup agent, the SSH daemon, administrators logging in. If any of them can read or modify any file, then a vulnerability in the least important one compromises everything: the database password in your config, the private TLS key, the SSH host keys. Unix permissions are the oldest, simplest mechanism for limiting what each process can touch, and they still do most of the work on a modern server.

Every process runs as a user (a numeric UID) and belongs to one primary group plus supplementary groups (GIDs). Every file has an owner user and an owner group. Names map to numbers through /etc/passwd and /etc/group ; the kernel only knows the numbers, which is why files copied between machines or into containers sometimes show odd ownership. id # uid=1000(deploy) gid=1000(deploy) groups=1000(deploy),27(sudo),999(docker) getent passwd app # app:x:1001:1001::/srv/app:/usr/sbin/nologin sudo useradd --system --home /srv/app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app # service account sudo usermod -aG docker deploy # add to a supplementary group (log out/in to take effect) Two kinds of users matter on a server: - Human users ( deploy , alice ): log in via SSH keys, have a shell, use sudo for privileged actions, and are individually identifiable in logs. Shared accounts destroy accountability. - Service users ( app , postgres , www-data ): own and run a specific service, have no password and no login shell, and own only the files that service needs. root (UID 0) bypasses all permission checks. Nothing you run routinely should be root. Services that must bind privileged ports (below 1024) get the specific capability instead ( CAP NET BIND SERVICE via systemd's AmbientCapabilities= ) or sit behind a reverse proxy that handles port 443.

ls -l shows a ten-character mode such as -rwxr-x--- . The first character is the type ( - file, d directory, l symlink). Then three triplets for user (owner), group , and others : read, write, execute. value For files : r read contents, w modify, x execute as a program. For directories the meanings change, and this trips people up: r list entry names, w create, delete or rename entries (regardless of the file's own permissions!), x traverse: enter the directory and access entries by name. A directory with r but no x lets you see names but not open them; with x but no r you can open a file if you already know its name. Octal notation sums r=4, w=2, x=1 per triplet: rw-r----- is 640. Common production modes: Mode Use --- --- 600 Private keys, .env files, secrets. Owner only. 640 Config readable by the service group (e.g. owned root:app ). 644 Public static files, most source code. 700 Private directories such as ~/.ssh . 750 Application directories: owner full, group traverse/read. 755 Executables and public directories. 1777 /tmp : world-writable with the sticky bit (see below). chmod -R 777 makes every file readable, writable and executable by everyone on the system. Any compromised process can then read your secrets and replace your code. It also usually does not fix the actual problem, which is almost always wrong ownership . Fix ownership with chown , then set sensible modes. :::

- setuid (4000) on an executable: run with the file owner's privileges. /usr/bin/passwd is setuid root so users can change their own password. Never set it on your own scripts; it is a classic privilege-escalation vector. The kernel ignores setuid on scripts for this reason. - setgid (2000) on a directory: new files inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group. Useful for shared deploy directories so files created by deploy are owned by group app . - sticky (1000) on a directory: only a file's owner can delete or rename it, even if the directory is world-writable. This is what makes /tmp safe for multiple users. sudo chmod 2775 /srv/app/shared # setgid: files created here get group 'app' ls -ld /srv/app/shared # drwxrwsr-x

New files are created with permissions masked by the process's umask . Default 022 yields 644 for files and 755 for directories; 077 yields 600/700. Service units can set UMask=0027 so an application never accidentally creates world-readable files (uploaded documents, exported reports).

A layout that works for most single-server deployments: /srv/app/ root:app 750 # code; the service can read, not write /srv/app/current -> releases/2026-03-01 # symlink switched on deploy /srv/app/releases/ deploy:app 750 # deploy user writes new releases /srv/app/shared/uploads/ app:app 750 # the only place the app writes /etc/app/app.env root:app 640 # secrets: readable by the app group, not writable by the app /var/log/app/ app:app 750 # if not using journald Principles embedded there: 1. The application cannot modify its own code. If an attacker achieves code execution through a bug, they cannot persist by editing files. (Immutable container images give this for free.) 2. Secrets are readable, not writable, by the service , and unreadable by everyone else. 3. Writes are confined to a directory that holds only data, served with no execute permission and never interpreted as code. 4. Deployment uses a different user from the one that runs the service.

Classic permissions have one owner and one group. When that is not enough, POSIX ACLs add per-user and per-group entries ( setfacl -m u:backup:r /var/lib/pg dumps , inspect with getfacl ). Mandatory access control systems (SELinux on RHEL-family, AppArmor on Ubuntu) add kernel-enforced policies that confine even root-owned services; a web server confined by SELinux cannot read /home regardless of file modes. When something is denied and permissions look right, check ausearch -m avc (SELinux) or dmesg grep apparmor .

t: Processes, Threads, Signals and System Calls
x: Every deployment, scale-down and crash recovery is a story about processes being told to stop and new ones starting. If your service does not handle that conversation properly, every deploy drops requests, corrupts a batch job, or leaves database connections dangling. "We see errors for 30 seconds on every release" is nearly always a signal-handling problem.

t: Processes, Threads, Signals and System Calls
x: A process is created by fork (the kernel clones the calling process) followed usually by exec (replacing the clone's program with a new one). The parent can wait for the child to finish and collect its exit status : 0 means success, anything else is failure by convention. Shells, systemd, Gunicorn and container runtimes all follow this pattern. Exit codes you will meet: Code Meaning --- --- 0 Success 1, 2 Generic errors (application-defined) 126 / 127 Not executable / command not found (shell) 128 + N Killed by signal N: 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL, often the OOM killer), 143 = 128+15 (SIGTERM), 139 = 128+11 (SIGSEGV, a crash) So when ECS or Kubernetes reports a container exited with 137, the kernel killed it, usually for exceeding memory. 143 means it was asked to stop and complied. 1 means it decided to exit itself; read its logs. When a process exits before its parent has waited for it, it becomes a zombie : a dead entry in the process table holding only its exit status. Zombies are harmless individually but a parent that never reaps children leaks process table entries. When a parent dies first, children are orphaned and adopted by PID 1, which must reap them. This is why PID 1 in a container matters (below).

t: Processes, Threads, Signals and System Calls
x: Threads are execution contexts within one process sharing its memory, file descriptors and signals. The kernel schedules threads, not processes. One misbehaving thread (infinite loop, deadlock) does not kill the process but can consume a core or hold a lock forever. Signals are delivered to the process and handled by whichever thread is not blocking them, which is why most runtimes handle signals in the main thread.

x: Inside a container the first process is PID 1 and inherits two special duties: it must reap orphaned zombies, and the kernel does not apply default signal actions to it, so an unhandled SIGTERM is simply ignored. Two consequences: 1. CMD python app.py gives your app PID 1. Fine if it handles SIGTERM. Fixes: use the exec form ( CMD ["python", "app.py"] ), use exec in entrypoint scripts ( exec gunicorn ... ), or run a tiny init such as tini ( docker run --init , or ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"] ). - Distinguish virtual memory, resident memory, shared memory and page cache, and read free , top and cgroup statistics correctly. - Explain heap versus stack, garbage collection, and why memory usage grows after deployment. - Predict and prevent out-of-memory kills in containers, including the JVM and Node heap-sizing traps. - Diagnose a memory leak methodically. ::: Chapters 2, 3 and 6. :::

Memory failures are abrupt. CPU saturation makes things slow; memory exhaustion makes things die. A container that exceeds its limit is killed with no stack trace, the orchestrator restarts it, it serves traffic for twenty minutes and dies again, and the on-call engineer sees "healthy, restarting" in a loop. Understanding memory is how you turn that from a mystery into a ten-minute fix.

A process's address space contains: - Text : the program's machine code, read-only, shared between processes running the same binary. - Data and BSS : global variables. - Heap : dynamically allocated objects. Grows and shrinks as the runtime allocates ( malloc / new ) and frees. In garbage-collected runtimes, this is where your objects live. - Stack : one per thread, holding local variables and call frames. Typically 8 MB maximum per thread on Linux; a thousand threads reserve 8 GB of virtual space (not physical). Deep recursion overflows it. - Memory-mapped files and shared libraries : libc , the runtime's .so files, and any files mapped with mmap . Shared across processes. All of this is virtual : addresses the process uses, mapped by the kernel to physical pages on first touch. Memory the process reserved but never touched costs nothing physical. This is why VSZ (virtual size) is nearly meaningless for capacity planning and RSS (resident set size) is what matters, with the caveat that RSS double-counts shared pages across processes. PSS (proportional set size, in /proc/ /smaps rollup ) divides shared pages fairly. ps -o pid,rss,vsz,cmd -p $(pgrep -d, -f gunicorn) # RSS in KB grep -E 'Rss|Pss|Swap' /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup

h: Garbage collection and why memory grows after deploy
x: In Python, Node, Java and Go, you allocate and the runtime frees unreachable objects. Two behaviours surprise people: 1. Runtimes keep freed memory. Allocators request memory from the kernel in large chunks and rarely return it. A process that briefly needed 800 MB will often stay at 800 MB RSS. Growth that plateaus is normal; growth that never plateaus is a leak. 2. Garbage collection is lazy and heuristic. Collectors run when allocation pressure reaches a threshold, not continuously. A JVM will happily grow its heap to the configured maximum before collecting aggressively. Memory graphs with a sawtooth pattern are healthy. A memory leak in a GC language means objects remain reachable when they should not: an ever-growing list used as a cache, event listeners never removed, per-request data stored on a global, closures capturing large objects, unbounded lru cache without maxsize . The classic symptom is RSS climbing linearly with request count and resetting only on restart.

Linux uses free RAM to cache files. free -h : total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 15Gi 4.2Gi 1.1Gi 120Mi 10Gi 10Gi Only 4.2 GB is used by processes; 10 GB is cache that will be reclaimed instantly when needed; available (10 GB) is the number to alert on. Databases depend on this cache heavily: PostgreSQL's performance on a server with lots of free RAM comes largely from the kernel caching table files.

Swap is disk used as overflow memory. On servers it is a double-edged sword: it prevents OOM kills during brief spikes, but a server that is actively swapping becomes unusably slow, and a sluggish database is often worse than a restarted one. Many cloud images ship with no swap; Kubernetes historically required swap off. For a small client VM, a modest swap file with low vm.swappiness (10) is a reasonable safety net; for containers, rely on limits and right-sizing instead.

A container's memory limit is a cgroup limit. When the processes in the cgroup exceed it, the kernel's oom killer kills a process inside the container; the container runtime reports exit code 137 and OOMKilled: true . Three things to know: - The cgroup counts more than your heap : it includes every process in the container, their stacks, shared libraries (counted once per cgroup), and, in cgroup v1, file page cache attributable to the container. Headroom of 25–40% above steady-state RSS is a sensible starting point. - Runtimes may not see the limit. Older JVMs sized their default heap from the host's memory and were killed for using it; modern JVMs (11+) are container-aware and default to 25% of the cgroup limit, which is usually too small, so set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 . Node's default heap cap (roughly 2–4 GB depending on version and architecture) may exceed a small container's limit; set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the limit in megabytes. Python has no heap cap at all; your worker count is the control. - Requests versus limits. Kubernetes lets you request less than you limit. Memory is not compressible: if the node runs out, pods using more than their request are the first evicted. Set memory request equal to limit for predictable services. # Inside a container: what is my limit and usage? (cgroup v2) cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max # bytes, or "max" cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events # oom_kill counter # From the host / orchestrator

A method that works: 1. Measure RSS of one worker at idle and after a sustained load test (Part XI chapter 8) at target concurrency. 2. Total memory ≈ workers × per-worker peak RSS + runtime baseline + 25–40% headroom. 3. Set the container limit to that total and the worker count to match. For Gunicorn with 4 async workers at 150 MB peak each: 600 MB + headroom ≈ 800 MB to 1 GB. 4. Alert at 80% of the limit and on any OOM kill event. 5. Re-measure after major dependency upgrades; memory profiles change.

- Raising the memory limit repeatedly instead of finding the leak. - Running the JVM in a container without MaxRAMPercentage , or Node without --max-old-space-size . - Alerting on "used" memory including page cache. - Setting Kubernetes memory requests far below limits, inviting eviction of the busiest pods. - Unbounded in-process caches and per-request data stored globally. - Loading an entire file or query result into memory when streaming would do. questions A process shows VSZ 6.2 GB and RSS 310 MB. How much physical memory is it using? options 6.2 GB About 310 MB (less if shared pages are counted fairly) 6.5 GB Cannot be determined answer explain VSZ is reserved address space; RSS is resident physical memory. PSS refines RSS by sharing shared pages across processes. Why might a Java service be OOM-killed in a 2 GB container while reporting a 1.5 GB heap? options The JVM lies The cgroup counts heap plus metaspace, thread stacks, JIT code cache, native buffers and off-heap memory Java cannot run in containers The limit is applied to the host answer explain Heap is only part of a JVM's footprint. Leave headroom and tune MaxRAMPercentage. Memory on a pod grows linearly under steady traffic and only drops on restart. What is this? options Normal GC behaviour A memory leak: objects remain reachable Page cache Swap usage answer explain GC heaps plateau or saw-tooth. Unbounded linear growth means reachable garbage. Which `free` column should a memory alert be based on? options a

- Separate code, configuration and secrets, and explain why each lives in a different place. - Load, validate and type-check configuration at start-up so a misconfigured service fails immediately and loudly. - Manage configuration across development, staging and production without duplicating secrets. - Avoid the leaks and outages that configuration causes. ::: Chapters 4 and 6. :::

The same code must run on a laptop, in CI, in staging and in production, each with a different database, different credentials, different feature toggles and different log levels. Hard-coding any of those into the source means a rebuild per environment and secrets in Git. The twelve-factor app principle, "store config in the environment", became standard because it solved both problems at once: the artifact is identical everywhere and the environment supplies what differs. Configuration is also a leading cause of incidents. A missing variable in one environment, a trailing newline in a secret, a URL that points at production from staging, a default that was fine on a laptop and catastrophic at scale. The techniques in this chapter are about making those failures impossible or immediate.

Category Examples Where it lives Changes --- --- --- --- Code Business logic, routes, defaults that never vary The repository Per release Configuration Database host, log level, feature flags, external URLs, worker count Environment variables, config files, parameter store Per environment, occasionally at runtime Secrets Database password, API keys, signing keys, TLS private keys Secrets manager, injected at runtime Rotated on schedule or compromise Configuration can live in version control (one file per environment, no secrets). Secrets must never be in version control, images, logs or error reports, and ideally never on disk in plain text.

Every process has a set of name=value strings inherited from its parent. They are simple, universal, and supported by every runtime and platform (systemd Environment= , Docker -e , ECS task definitions, Kubernetes env , Lambda configuration). export DATABASE_URL='postgresql://app:secret@db.internal:5432/app?sslmode=require' export LOG_LEVEL=info python -c 'import os; print(os.environ["LOG_LEVEL"])' Limitations to design around: - Strings only. Numbers, booleans and lists must be parsed. DEBUG=false is a non-empty string and therefore truthy in naive code. - Visible to the process tree. Child processes inherit them; /proc/ /environ exposes them to the same user and root; crash reporters and debug pages may dump them. Secrets in environment variables are acceptable in containers but less safe than file or API injection. - No structure. Nested configuration becomes DB POOL MAX SIZE -style names. - Set at start. Changing them requires a restart, which is also a feature: configuration becomes part of the deployment and is auditable.

A .env file holds KEY=value lines loaded into the environment by a library ( python-dotenv , dotenv in Node) or by Docker Compose. Rules: - .env is for local development only and is in .gitignore . Commit a .env.example with every key and a placeholder value so new developers know what to set. - Production does not use .env files; the platform injects variables (and secrets come from a secrets manager). - Quote values containing spaces or ; beware of trailing whitespace and Windows line endings, which have caused countless "invalid password" incidents. # .env.example — copy to .env and fill in DATABASE_URL=postgresql://app:password@localhost:5432/app REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0 SECRET_KEY=change-me-generate-with-openssl-rand-hex-32 LOG_LEVEL=debug STRIPE_API_KEY=sk_test_xxx ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3000

The single most effective practice: parse all configuration into a typed object at start-up and refuse to start if anything is missing or malformed. A service that starts with a bad config and fails on the first request is far worse than one that crashes immediately with a clear message, because the orchestrator will keep the broken version "healthy" while users suffer. # app/config.py — pydantic-settings (FastAPI ecosystem) from pydantic import Field, PostgresDsn, AnyHttpUrl, SecretStr, field_validator from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict class Settings(BaseSettings): model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_file_encoding="utf-8", extra="forbid") env: str = Field(pattern="^(dev|staging|prod)$") database_url: PostgresDsn redis_url: str secret_key: SecretStr = Field(min_length=32) log_level: str = "info" allowed_origins: list[AnyHttpUrl] = [] db_pool_size: int = Field(default=10, ge=1, le=100) request_timeout_s: float = 30.0 stripe_api_key: SecretStr | None = None @field_validator("allowed_origins", mode="before") @classmethod def split_csv(cls, v): return [x.strip() for x in v.split(",")] if isinstance(v, str) else v settings = Settings() # raises a precise ValidationError listing every problem // config.js — zod in Node import { z } from 'zod'; const schema = z.object({ NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'staging', 'production']), PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(8000), DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(), SECRET_KEY: z

A typical order, highest priority first: command-line flags → environment variables → environment-specific file → defaults in code. Keep it simple and document it. Resist building a configuration system with six layers; nobody will remember which wins.

h: Secrets: where they come from in production
x: The progression from unsafe to safe: 1. Hard-coded in source. Never. 2. In a .env file on the server with mode 600. Acceptable for a single small VM if the file is not in Git and backups are encrypted; weak audit trail and rotation. 3. Platform-injected environment variables from a secrets manager (ECS secrets referencing Secrets Manager or Parameter Store; Kubernetes Secrets, ideally synced from an external store). The orchestrator fetches at start and the application just reads os.environ . Standard for containers. 4. Fetched by the application at start-up via SDK using an iam role (no credentials needed to get credentials). Enables rotation without redeploy, fine-grained audit of every read, and keeps secrets out of the environment entirely. 5. Short-lived credentials generated on demand (IAM database authentication, Vault dynamic secrets). The strongest model; more moving parts. Part IV chapter 17 and Part VII chapter 12 cover the tooling. Whatever the mechanism, the application should receive secrets through one well-defined path and never log them.

Some configuration must change without a restart: turning a feature off during an incident, adjusting a rate limit, enabling a new checkout for 5% of users. That is a feature flag system (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, AWS AppConfig, or a database table with a cache). Keep the distinction: start-up config is validated once and immutable; runtime flags are read per request from a cached source with a safe default if the source is unreachable.

Environments should differ only in configuration values, never in code paths. Code that says if env == "prod": do something different() is a bug waiting to be found only in production. The acceptable exceptions are observability settings (log level, sampling rate) and safety rails (refuse to run destructive migrations when env == "prod" without a flag).

- Missing variable with a silent default. os.environ.get("DATABASE URL", "postgresql://localhost/dev") connects staging to a local database that does not exist, or worse, exists. - Secrets in build arguments. docker build --build-arg API KEY=... embeds the key in image history ( docker history shows it). Use BuildKit secret mounts. - Secrets in logs. Logging the full config object, or an HTTP client logging request headers including Authorization . - Trailing newline in a secret copied from a file into a console. The password is hunter2\n . Strip on load, and prefer programmatic secret creation. - Same secret across environments. A leaked staging key is a production key. - Environment variable injection via .env in a public static directory , served by the web server. Never place .env under the web root. - Config drift between instances : two servers in a fleet with different values because someone edited one by hand. questions Why should a service refuse to start when a required environment variable is missing, rather than defaulting? options Defaults are slower A loud, immediate failure is diagnosed in seconds; a silent default fails later, confusingly, or dangerously Environment variables cannot have defaults Orchestrators require it answer explain Fail fast. A service that starts in a broken state passes health checks and causes harder-to-trace incidents. Where should production database passwords live? options In a .env file committed to the repo In the Dockerfile as ENV

Then add secret scanning (Part X chapter 3). 3. Design the configuration matrix for an application with three environments: list every key, which environment it varies in, and whether it is a secret.

t: Package Managers, Dependencies and Reproducible Builds
x: A modern application is mostly other people's code. A typical FastAPI service pulls in 60 to 120 packages; a React frontend over a thousand. Each is a version chosen by someone, downloadable from a registry you do not control, with transitive dependencies of its own. Three failure modes follow: 1. "Works on my machine." Your laptop resolved requests =2.28 to 2.31 in March; the CI runner resolved it to 2.32 in June and something changed. 2. Breaking changes on rebuild. A production hotfix rebuilds the image, picks up a new minor version of a library, and ships an unrelated regression. 3. Supply chain compromise. A maintainer account is hijacked and a malicious version is published; everyone who installs "the latest compatible version" that day is affected. Lockfiles and reproducible builds address the first two. The third requires those plus scanning and discipline (Part IV chapter 20).

t: Package Managers, Dependencies and Reproducible Builds
x: A lockfile records the exact resolved version of every package, direct and transitive, with integrity hashes: package-lock.json , pnpm-lock.yaml , yarn.lock , poetry.lock , uv.lock , Pipfile.lock , Cargo.lock , go.sum . Installing from a lockfile skips resolution and installs precisely what is recorded, failing if a hash does not match. Rules: - Commit the lockfile for applications. (Libraries typically do not, so consumers can resolve against their own trees.) - Install from the lockfile in CI and Docker , in a mode that refuses to update it: npm ci (not npm install ), pnpm install --frozen-lockfile , poetry install --sync / uv sync --locked , pip install -r requirements.txt where the file was generated with hashes by pip-compile --generate-hashes . - Update deliberately , in their own pull requests, with tests, not as a side effect of adding a feature. # Python with uv (fast, lockfile-based) uv init && uv add "fastapi>=0.110" "sqlalchemy>=2" "psycopg[binary]" uv lock # writes uv.lock with exact versions and hashes uv sync --locked # CI/Docker: install exactly, fail if lock is stale # Python with pip-tools pip-compile --generate-hashes -o requirements.txt pyproject.toml pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt # Node npm ci # exact install from package-lock.json; errors if out of sync

t: Package Managers, Dependencies and Reproducible Builds
x: A build is reproducible when the same source produces the same artifact regardless of when or where it runs. Lockfiles handle application dependencies. The remaining variables: - Runtime version. Pin it: FROM python:3.12.7-slim-bookworm , .nvmrc / engines , .python-version . Better, pin the base image by digest: FROM python:3.12.7-slim@sha256:... , because tags are mutable and 3.12-slim today is not 3.12-slim next month. - System packages. apt-get install -y libpq5=16.4-1 pins; unpinned apt installs drift. Many teams accept apt drift but rebuild from scratch regularly and scan the result. - Build tools. The compiler, bundler, and their plugins are dependencies too; lock them. - Time and randomness. Timestamps embedded in artifacts break bit-for-bit reproducibility; SOURCE DATE EPOCH and deterministic bundler settings fix it. For most teams, "same versions of everything" is sufficient; bit-identical outputs matter for high-assurance supply chain verification. # Pinned, reproducible Python image (excerpt) FROM python:3.12.7-slim-bookworm@sha256:2b5d3a1b2f2b9c2d4e4e8c6d1c8b1a0f5e6d7c8b9a0f1e2d3c4b5a6f7e8d9c0b AS base ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.4.18 /uv /usr/local/bin/uv WORKDIR /app COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./ RUN uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project COPY . . (The digest above is illustrative; obtain the real one with docker pull and docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' .)

t: Git Workflows, Branching, Pull Requests and Releases
x: A pull request is a unit of change, a review conversation and a permanent record. Make all three good: - Small. Under 400 changed lines reviews well; 2,000-line PRs get rubber-stamped. Split refactors from behaviour changes. - Described. What changed, why, how it was tested, what reviewers should focus on, screenshots for UI, links to the ticket and any ADR. A template helps. - Self-reviewed first. Read your own diff before requesting review; you will catch half the comments yourself. - Reviewed for the right things : correctness, security (input validation, authorization, secrets), operability (logging, metrics, migrations), tests, clarity. Style is for linters. Part XII chapter 6 covers review in depth. - Merged cleanly. Squash-merge for feature branches gives one meaningful commit per PR on main ; rebase-merge keeps individual commits if they are curated. Avoid merge commits from main into the feature branch cluttering history; rebase the branch instead. Commit messages: a short imperative subject line under 72 characters, a blank line, then the why. If the only place your code runs with real infrastructure is production, then production is where you discover that the migration locks a table for ten minutes, that the new library needs a system package the image lacks, or that the load balancer's health check path changed. Environments exist to move those discoveries earlier, to a place where they cost nothing. But environments are expensive to run and easy to let rot. A staging environment that differs from production in a dozen unknown ways gives false confidence, which is worse than none.

Environment Purpose Who uses it Data --- --- --- --- Local / development Fast iteration, debugging Each engineer Synthetic, seeded CI / ephemeral Automated tests on every PR; disposable Pipelines Fixtures, test containers Preview / per-PR (optional) Review a feature in a live deployment before merge Reviewers, product, client Synthetic Staging / pre-production Final rehearsal: production-like infra, integration with real third-party sandboxes, migration dry run, acceptance testing Team, QA, client Anonymised or synthetic; never raw production PII Production Real users Everyone Real Some clients add UAT (user acceptance testing) as a separate stable environment where their staff validate releases on their own schedule, or a DR environment that mirrors production in another region. Resist adding environments without a clear question each one answers.

The principle: same artifact, same infrastructure shape, different configuration . Must match production: - The container image or build artifact (promote the exact image; never rebuild). - Runtime and dependency versions (guaranteed by the artifact). - Database engine and major version (PostgreSQL 16 in prod, PostgreSQL 16 in staging; SQLite locally is a trap). - Infrastructure topology: load balancer, private subnets, the same managed services, IAM roles with equivalent policies. Smaller instance sizes are fine; different kinds of components are not. - Configuration keys : every variable production needs exists in staging with a staging value. - Deployment mechanism: the same pipeline deploys to both; staging is the rehearsal of the production deploy. May differ: - Instance sizes, replica counts, autoscaling bounds (cost). - Secrets and credentials (always different). - External endpoints (payment sandbox versus live). - Log verbosity and sampling. - Domain names and certificates ( staging-api.client.com ). Infrastructure as code (Part X) is what makes parity achievable: the same Terraform module with a different variables file produces structurally identical environments.

Copying the production database to staging is the fastest way to leak client data. Staging is less protected, more people have access, it is forgotten in backups, and nobody notices when a developer exports it to a laptop. Rules: 1. Never copy raw production data containing personal information to a lower environment without a documented anonymisation step and the client's agreement. 2. Prefer synthetic data generators that produce realistic volumes and shapes (Faker, custom seeders) and are committed with the code. 3. When production-like data is genuinely required (performance testing, reproducing a bug), use a masking pipeline : restore to an isolated database, run deterministic masking (replace names, emails, addresses, free text; preserve referential integrity and distributions), verify no PII remains, then load into staging. Automate and audit it. 4. Payment, health and regulated data: synthetic only, no exceptions. Part IV chapter 23 covers the obligations behind this.

Changes move upward: a merge to main deploys to staging automatically; a production deploy is triggered by promotion of the same artifact after checks. Patterns: - Automatic to staging, manual approval to production (GitHub Environments with required reviewers). Most client projects. - Fully automatic with canary when the team has strong observability and rollback automation. - Scheduled release trains when the client needs predictability (every Tuesday 10:00) or change-management approval. The promotion step is where the audit trail lives: who approved, which artifact, which commit, when. Part X chapter 9.

Staging decays silently. Guard it: - Deploy to staging on every merge, so it is never behind by more than one change. - Run smoke tests and synthetic checks against staging just like production. - Apply the same infrastructure code; forbid console changes in staging too. - Periodically rebuild staging from scratch with the IaC to prove the code is complete (this also tests disaster recovery). - Budget for it honestly. A staging environment at 20–30% of production cost is typical; cutting it to zero is a false economy on anything that matters.

Spinning up a complete environment per pull request (preview deployments) lets reviewers and clients click through a feature before merge. Feasible when infrastructure is code and cheap (containers, serverless, a shared database with per-PR schemas). Destroy on merge to control cost. Even without full previews, running integration tests against disposable containers in CI (Testcontainers, Docker Compose) captures most of the value.

The local environment should mirror production services through Docker Compose (same database engine, Redis, message broker) while the application runs natively or in a container with hot reload. A make dev or docker compose up that works from a fresh clone in under five minutes is a strong signal of a healthy project; new team members and client engineers judge you by it. # docker-compose.yml (development) services: db: image: postgres:16.4 environment: { POSTGRES_USER: app, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app, POSTGRES_DB: app } ports: ["5432:5432"] volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"] healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"], interval: 5s, retries: 10 } redis: image: redis:7.4-alpine ports: ["6379:6379"] api: build: { context: ., target: dev } command: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --reload env_file: .env volumes: [".:/app"] ports: ["8000:8000"] depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy }, redis: { condition: service_started } } volumes: { pgdata: {} }

Artifact and topology parity is the point. A developer wants to copy the production database to staging to debug a report. What should happen? options Copy it; staging is internal Refuse, or use an automated, verified anonymisation pipeline with the client's agreement Copy it but delete it afterwards Copy only the last month answer explain Lower environments have weaker controls. Raw PII must not move downward without masking and consent. - Apply semantic versioning correctly to libraries, services and APIs, and know when it does not apply. - Produce releases with changelogs, tags and artifacts that can be traced from a running system back to source. - Design a deprecation policy for APIs consumed by clients. - Coordinate releases of interdependent components without breaking consumers. ::: Chapters 9 and 10. :::

Version numbers are a communication protocol between producers and consumers of software. If 2.3.1 to 2.4.0 might break my integration, I must read every changelog and test every upgrade; if the convention guarantees it will not, I can upgrade with confidence. Release management is the discipline that makes the guarantee true, and that lets anyone answer "what exactly is running, and what changed since last week?"

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , with optional pre-release ( 2.0.0-rc.1 ) and build metadata ( +build.42 ): - PATCH : backward-compatible bug fixes. Consumers upgrade freely. - MINOR : backward-compatible new functionality. Consumers upgrade freely; may adopt new features. - MAJOR : incompatible changes. Consumers must read the migration guide and change code. 0.y.z means "anything may change". Many projects stay there far too long; once anyone depends on you in production, release 1.0 and honour the contract. What counts as breaking? For a library: removing or renaming a public function, changing a signature or return type, tightening accepted inputs, changing default behaviour, raising the minimum runtime version. For an HTTP API: removing a field or endpoint, renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional parameter required, changing error codes clients depend on, changing authentication. Adding fields, endpoints, optional parameters and enum values is usually compatible if consumers were told to ignore unknown fields and handle unknown enum values; say so in your API documentation.

A deployed service has one version running at a time (or two, during rollout), chosen by you. Its consumers do not pick a version; they get whatever is deployed. So the service's build version (often just the Git SHA or a date-based tag like 2026.03.14.1 ) is for traceability, while its API version ( /v1/ , /v2/ ) is the contract consumers depend on. Part III chapter 2 covers API versioning in depth. Do not confuse the two: bumping the build version on every deploy is right; bumping the API version on every deploy is a disaster. Libraries, SDKs, CLI tools, Terraform modules, Helm charts and container base images that others consume follow semantic versioning strictly.

A release ties together: a Git tag, a changelog entry, built artifacts (container image, wheel, zip) with immutable identifiers, and a record of where and when it was deployed. Make the chain visible: # Tag and build git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0" git push origin v2.4.0 docker build -t registry/app:2.4.0 -t registry/app:sha-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \ --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD) \ --label org.opencontainers.image.version=2.4.0 . # /version endpoint: a production system should be able to say what it is @app.get("/version") def version(): return {"version": settings.app_version, "commit": settings.git_sha, "built_at": settings.build_time} The labels and the endpoint are populated at build time from the pipeline. During an incident, "which version is running?" should be answerable with one curl , not by asking around.

Keep CHANGELOG.md in the "Keep a Changelog" format: sections per version with Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write for the consumer: what they will notice and what they must do. Automation (Conventional Commits with tools like release-please or semantic-release ) can derive versions and changelog entries from commit messages like feat: , fix: , feat!: , which also forces thought about compatibility at commit time. Release notes for clients are a different document: fewer internals, more "what this means for you", written by a human.

When a client integrates against your API, removing anything becomes a negotiation. Publish a policy up front: 1. Mark deprecated elements in documentation and responses ( Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers; @deprecated in SDKs). 2. Announce with a date and a migration path; log usage of deprecated features so you know who is still calling them. 3. Maintain the deprecated behaviour for a stated period (commonly 6–12 months for external APIs; shorter for internal ones). 4. Remove in a major version, after confirming usage is zero or stakeholders have signed off.

Frontend, backend and database rarely change in lockstep. Rules that keep rollouts safe: - Backend before frontend : the API must accept the new requests before any client sends them, and keep accepting old ones until all clients have moved. - Expand, then contract for databases: add columns and tables first (compatible with old code), deploy code that uses them, then remove old columns in a later release (Part X chapter 8). - Tolerant readers : consumers ignore unknown fields; producers never remove fields without the deprecation process. - Feature flags decouple deploy from release: ship the code dark, enable when all parts are in place.

Frequent small releases are safer than rare large ones: each carries less change, is easier to review, and if it fails, the suspect set is small. Teams deploying many times a day have lower change-failure rates than teams deploying monthly, not despite the frequency but because of what frequency forces: automation, small batches, good rollback. For clients who require scheduled releases, keep the internal cadence high (staging continuously) and batch only the production promotion.

Every release needs an answer to "how do we undo this?" Rolling back the application means deploying the previous artifact, which must still exist and still be compatible with the current database schema (this is why migrations are expand-first). Rolling forward means fixing quickly and releasing a new version; sensible when the fix is obvious and rollback is risky. Decide which applies before deploying, and write it in the deployment ticket.

- Define the three architectural styles precisely and describe the operational cost of each. - Recognise when microservices solve a real problem and when they create one. - Design a modular monolith that can be split later without a rewrite. - Advise a client honestly on which style fits their team and constraints. ::: Chapters 1 and 11. :::

How you divide a system into deployable units determines how you build, test, deploy, scale, secure and debug it for years. The industry oscillated from monoliths to microservices and partly back, leaving many teams with distributed systems they did not need and cannot operate. Architecture should follow the problem and the team, not the conference circuit.

One codebase, one deployable, one process (or identical replicas of it), typically one database. Internal calls are function calls. A FastAPI application with routers for users, orders and billing, deployed as one container, is a monolith. Strengths: simplest to develop, test, deploy and debug; transactions across features are trivial; refactoring across boundaries is an IDE operation; one set of infrastructure to secure and monitor. Weaknesses: everything scales together (the PDF generator and the login endpoint share CPU); one bad deploy affects everything; large teams step on each other; the codebase can degrade into a tangle if modules are not enforced; a single runtime and language.

Still one deployable, but internally divided into modules with explicit boundaries: each module owns its tables, exposes a small interface, and is forbidden (by convention and by tooling) from reaching into another module's internals. Communication between modules goes through those interfaces, sometimes through in-process events. This captures most of the organisational benefits claimed for microservices (clear ownership, independent evolution, enforced contracts) with none of the distributed-systems cost. It is also the best preparation for extracting a service later, because the seams already exist.

Many independently deployable services, each owning its data, communicating over the network (HTTP, gRPC, messages). Each can use its own language, scale independently and be deployed by its own team on its own schedule. What you pay for that: every call across a boundary can fail, time out or be slow; data consistency across services needs sagas or eventual consistency instead of a transaction; debugging requires distributed tracing; each service needs its own pipeline, monitoring, secrets, scaling policy and on-call ownership; local development needs a way to run or mock a dozen services; versioning of inter-service contracts becomes a permanent concern; and the network itself must be secured service-to-service. Netflix-scale organisations absorb this with platform teams. A five-person team cannot. title The same features, three ways intro Click components to see what changes. Note where the network (and therefore failure) appears. nodes label Monolith users + orders + billing One process. A request to create an order calls billing.charge() as a function and writes users, orders and billing tables in one transaction. label One database Shared schema. Joins across features are easy. Enforcing that modules do not read each other's tables is a discipline problem. label Modular monolith users | orders | billing modules One process, but orders calls billing only through billing's public interface. Lint rules or import boundaries forbid cross-module internals. Each module owns it

Real reasons, in rough order of frequency: 1. Organisational scale : many teams need to deploy independently without coordinating releases. Below roughly 30–50 engineers this rarely applies. 2. Radically different scaling or runtime needs : a GPU inference component, a high-throughput ingestion path, a legacy system in another language. 3. Isolation requirements : a component handling card data (PCI scope) or a tenant that requires physical separation. 4. Independent failure domains where part of the product must stay up when another part is down, and the team can build the resilience patterns that make that true. In the 1960s and 70s, networks were built by vendors and each spoke its own language: an IBM network could not talk to a DEC network. The research that became the Internet asked a different question: how do you connect networks of networks owned by different organisations, running different hardware, with no central operator, so that any machine can reach any other, and so that the system keeps working when parts of it fail? The answers shaped everything you deploy today: 1. Packet switching. Data is chopped into small, independently routed packets rather than reserving a circuit. Links are shared; failures reroute. 2. Layering. Each layer provides a service to the one above and relies on the one below, so a web application does not care whether the bytes cross fibre, Wi-Fi or a satellite. 3. The end-to-end principle. The network core does one thing (deliver packets, best effort). Reliability, ordering, encryption and application semantics live at the endpoints. This is why your server implements TCP and TLS logic, and a router does not. 4. Decentralised addressing and routing. Addresses are allocated hierarchically; routes are exchanged between independent networks by a protocol that assumes no one is in charge.

A packet is a bounded chunk of bytes with headers describing where it is going, where it came from, and what it contains. The maximum size a link can carry is its mtu, typically 1,500 bytes on Ethernet. A 100 KB JSON response therefore travels as roughly 70 packets, each of which may take a different path and arrive out of order, duplicated, delayed or not at all. TCP (chapter 6) hides this from your application by numbering and re-sending; UDP does not. They never leave the local network; a router strips this header and adds a new one for the next hop. Chapter 4. - A host is any endpoint: your laptop, a server, a phone, a load balancer. Hosts have IP addresses and run applications. - A switch connects hosts on the same local network (Layer 2). It learns which MAC address is on which port and forwards frames accordingly. It does not understand IP. - A router connects different networks (Layer 3). It looks at the destination IP, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet toward the next hop, rewriting the Layer 2 header. Your home router, your VPC's implicit router, and the core routers of an ISP all do this at different scales. - A gateway is simply the router a host sends to when the destination is not on its own network. In AWS these appear as abstractions: subnets are Layer 2 domains, the VPC router is implicit, an Internet Gateway is a router with NAT for public IPs, and security groups are firewalls attached to each host's virtual interface. Part VII chapter 5 maps them precisely.

The Internet is roughly 75,000 independently operated networks called autonomous systems (ASes), each with a number: AWS is AS16509 among others, Google AS15169, Cloudflare AS13335, your ISP has one too. ASes connect to each other through peering (exchanging traffic for free, usually at Internet exchange points) and transit (paying a larger provider to carry traffic to everyone else). Routes between ASes are exchanged with bgp, the Border Gateway Protocol. Each AS announces "I can reach 203.0.113.0/24" to its neighbours, who propagate it with their own AS prepended, building paths. Routers choose among paths by policy and length. BGP has no built-in authentication, which is why route leaks and hijacks occur (someone announces a prefix they do not own and traffic flows to them); RPKI is the slow fix being deployed. For an application engineer the practical lessons are: - Your users' path to you crosses networks you do not control, with latency and loss you do not control. Design for it (chapter 18). - Major outages are sometimes BGP incidents at a provider, not anything you did. Know how to check ( bgp.tools , provider status pages) before paging your whole team. - anycast lets CDNs and DNS providers announce the same prefix from dozens of locations; BGP routes each user to the nearest. This is how 1.1.1.1 is fast everywhere.

Networking is too complex to reason about all at once. Models divide it into layers with defined responsibilities and interfaces, so you can change one (swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet, HTTP/1.1 for HTTP/2) without touching the others. For an engineer the real value is diagnostic: a problem lives at one layer, and the tools and fixes differ completely per layer. "It does not work" becomes "DNS resolves, TCP connects, TLS fails with certificate error", which is a two-minute fix instead of a two-hour hunt.

The Internet's actual architecture uses four layers: Link (OSI 1–2), Internet (OSI 3), Transport (OSI 4), Application (OSI 5–7). When engineers say "Layer 4" or "Layer 7" they are using OSI numbers to talk about TCP/IP layers; the mixing is universal and harmless. Sending: the application hands a message to the transport layer, which adds a TCP header (making a segment); IP adds its header (packet); the link layer adds a frame header and trailer. Receiving reverses it. Each layer only reads its own header and passes the payload up. This is why: - A router can forward your HTTPS traffic without any ability to read it: it stops at Layer 3. - A security group can allow "TCP 443" without knowing whether the content is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2: it stops at Layer 4. - An ALB can route /api/ to one target group and /static/ to another: it decapsulates all the way to Layer 7, which requires terminating TLS (it must decrypt to read the path). - An NLB cannot route by path; it forwards TCP connections and is therefore faster, simpler and can pass TLS through untouched. That last contrast is the single most practically important consequence of layering for deployments, and chapter 13 builds on it.

Every host needs an address that routers can use to deliver packets. Addresses must be unique within the network they are routed in, allocated hierarchically so routing tables stay small, and divided into subnets that match physical or administrative boundaries. Getting the address plan wrong is one of the few infrastructure mistakes that is genuinely expensive to fix later: renumbering a VPC that peers with a client's network, or two merged companies both using 10.0.0.0/16 , costs weeks.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal octets: 203.0.113.7 . In binary: 203 .0 .113 .7 11001011 .00000000 .01110001 .00000111 There are 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out around 2011. The Internet still runs mostly on IPv4 thanks to nat and careful allocation.

10.0.1.0/24 means: the first 24 bits are the network prefix (fixed for every address in the block); the remaining 8 bits are the host part (vary within the block). The block therefore contains 2^8 = 256 addresses from 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255 . The subnet mask is the same information as 32 bits with 1s for the prefix: /24 is 255.255.255.0 , /16 is 255.255.0.0 , /20 is 255.255.240.0 . t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: IP addresses say where a packet should go. Something must decide how it gets there at each step, and physical networks deliver frames to hardware addresses, not IP addresses. Meanwhile, the world has far more devices than public IPv4 addresses, so most hosts use private addresses that cannot be routed on the Internet. Three mechanisms resolve this: routing tables choose the next hop, ARP finds its hardware address, and NAT bridges private and public address spaces.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
h: MAC addresses and the local segment
x: A MAC address ( 3c:22:fb:ab:cd:ef , 48 bits) identifies a network interface on its local segment: the set of hosts that can exchange Ethernet frames directly through switches without crossing a router. A subnet normally corresponds to one segment. MAC addresses are only meaningful locally; routers replace them at every hop. Switches build a table of which MAC address is reachable through which port by watching source addresses on incoming frames, and forward frames only to the right port. A frame to an unknown MAC is flooded to all ports; a frame to the broadcast MAC ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff reaches every host on the segment.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: A host that wants to send to 10.0.1.1 on its own subnet needs that host's MAC address. It broadcasts an ARP request ("who has 10.0.1.1?"), the owner replies ("10.0.1.1 is at 3c:22:…"), and the mapping is cached for a few minutes. ip neigh show # the ARP cache (Linux); 'arp -a' on older systems # 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 lladdr 0a:58:0a:00:01:01 REACHABLE ARP has no authentication: any host can claim any IP (ARP spoofing), which lets an attacker on the same segment intercept traffic. This is one reason switched, segmented networks and encrypted protocols matter even internally, and why cloud providers implement their own secured equivalents rather than real ARP. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (NDP) for the same purpose.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: Every host has a routing table. For each outgoing packet, the kernel finds the most specific matching route (longest prefix match) and uses it: ip route # default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100 # 10.0.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.1.57 # 172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.1 Reading it: packets to 10.0.1.0/24 go directly out eth0 (the destination is on-link; ARP for its MAC); packets to Docker's 172.17.0.0/16 go to the docker0 bridge; everything else ( default , i.e. 0.0.0.0/0 ) is sent to the gateway 10.0.1.1 , whose MAC is found by ARP. A packet to 8.8.8.8 therefore gets an Ethernet header addressed to the gateway and an IP header addressed to 8.8.8.8. Routers do the same with bigger tables. Core Internet routers hold about a million prefixes learned via BGP; your VPC router holds a handful of routes you define.
