An IP address identifies a host; a host runs many programs. Ports are the kernel's way of delivering a segment to the right one. Sockets are the programming interface over all of this. Nearly every "my service does not respond" or "connection refused" conversation is really about ports, bind addresses and socket states, so precision here pays off daily.

A port is a 16-bit number (0–65535) in the TCP or UDP header. By convention: - 0–1023 : well-known ports, require root or CAP NET BIND SERVICE to bind on Linux. 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 25/587 SMTP. - 1024–49151 : registered ports. 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 6379 Redis, 8080 alternative HTTP, 9090 Prometheus, 27017 MongoDB. - 49152–65535 (Linux default 32768–60999 ): ephemeral ports, assigned by the kernel to the client side of outgoing connections. TCP and UDP port spaces are independent: TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different endpoints (DNS uses both).

A socket is a kernel object a program creates to communicate, referenced by a file descriptor. Servers follow the sequence socket() → bind(address, port) → listen(backlog) → accept() in a loop; clients do socket() → connect(address, port) . Each accept() returns a new socket for that one client; the listening socket keeps listening. A TCP connection is uniquely identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). This is why one server port can hold thousands of simultaneous connections: each has a different client IP or client port. It also bounds the number of connections between one client IP and one server port to the number of ephemeral ports (about 28,000 on default Linux), which matters for proxies and load generators.

bind() takes an address as well as a port. The address decides which interfaces accept connections: - 127.0.0.1:8000 : only connections from the same host. Right for a database that only a local app uses, or a dev server. Wrong inside a container that must be reached from outside it , because the container's loopback is not the host's. - 0.0.0.0:8000 : all IPv4 interfaces. Standard for a service inside a container (the container's network namespace is already the isolation boundary) and for servers behind a firewall. - 10.0.1.57:8000 : one specific interface. Used on multi-homed hosts to listen only on the internal network. - [::]:8000 : all IPv6 interfaces (and usually IPv4 too, via dual-stack). The most common "it works locally but the container returns connection refused" bug is a server bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container. Docker's port mapping reaches the container's eth0 , not its loopback. Bind to 0.0.0.0 in containers. ::: Conversely, on a bare server with a public IP, binding a database or admin interface to 0.0.0.0 without a firewall exposes it to the Internet. Many breaches (exposed Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch instances) were simply default binds on public hosts.

ss -tan shows every TCP socket with its state. The ones that matter: State Meaning Operational note --- --- --- LISTEN Waiting for connections ss -ltnp lists them with the process SYN-SENT / SYN-RECV Handshake in progress Many SYN-RECV = backlog filling or SYN flood ESTABLISHED Open connection Count them per service for capacity FIN-WAIT / CLOSE-WAIT Closing Many CLOSE-WAIT = your application is not closing sockets after the peer did (leak) TIME-WAIT Closed, waiting ~60 s to ensure stray packets die Normal; thousands are fine; the side that closes first holds it ss -ltnp # listening sockets with process ss -tan state established | wc -l # open connections ss -tan | awk 'NR>1{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c # count by state ss -tn state established '( dport = :5432 )' # connections to PostgreSQL ss -s # summary

Connections that have completed the handshake but not yet been accept() ed queue in the backlog . Its size is the smaller of the application's listen() argument and the kernel's net.core.somaxconn (default 4096 on modern kernels, 128 on old ones). When it overflows, new connections are dropped (clients see slow connects or timeouts, not refusals). Signs: ss -ltn showing Recv-Q near Send-Q on a listening socket, and nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows increasing. Causes: the application is too slow to accept (event loop blocked, workers saturated). Raise the backlog as a stopgap; fix the saturation as the cure.

bind() fails if another socket already holds that address:port. Causes, in order of frequency: 1. The previous instance is still running. ss -ltnp grep :8000 shows the owner; stop it properly. 2. A connection in TIME-WAIT on that port after a restart. Servers set SO REUSEADDR so the listening socket can be rebound anyway; most frameworks do this for you. 3. A port mapping conflict in Docker : -p 8000:8000 when the host's 8000 is taken. Change the host side. 4. Two services configured with the same port by a copy-paste error in the unit file.

A process making many short-lived outbound connections to the same destination (a proxy without keep-alive, a load test, an app that opens a new database connection per request) runs out of ephemeral ports when the old ones sit in TIME-WAIT. Symptoms: connect(): Cannot assign requested address (EADDRNOTAVAIL) , latency spikes, intermittent failures. Fixes: reuse connections (HTTP keep-alive, connection pools), widen the range ( net.ipv4.ip local port range = 1024 65535 ), or enable net.ipv4.tcp tw reuse = 1 for outgoing connections. Through a NAT Gateway the same limit applies per destination at the gateway (chapter 4).

Every socket is a file descriptor. The per-process limit ( ulimit -n , often 1024 by default) caps connections; a busy proxy or WebSocket server needs tens of thousands. Set LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit, or ulimits in the container spec. Symptom: Too many open files , EMFILE , accept failures under load. If raising the limit only delays the error, you have a leak: connections not closed (see CLOSE-WAIT above).

Inside a container the process binds 0.0.0.0:8000 in its own network namespace. docker run -p 8080:8000 creates a DNAT rule from the host's 8080 to the container's 8000. In ECS with the awsvpc network mode, each task gets its own elastic network interface and IP, so the container port is reached directly on the task IP with no mapping; the ALB target group points at task-ip:8000 . In Kubernetes, a Service maps a stable virtual IP and port to pod IPs and container ports. Health checks follow the same rules: an ALB health check targets the task IP and the container port; it must hit a path the application serves on the interface it bound to.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: IP delivers packets unreliably and out of order. Applications want a reliable, ordered byte stream (a file transfer, an HTTP response) or, sometimes, fast delivery of small independent messages where a lost one should simply be forgotten (a voice packet, a DNS query). TCP and UDP are the two answers, and nearly everything else is built on one of them.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: UDP adds only ports and a checksum to IP. Each sendto() becomes one datagram; it may arrive, or not, in any order. No connection, no retransmission, no congestion control. Costs: none beyond IP. Used by DNS (small query, small answer; retry at the application), real-time media (a late packet is useless, so why retransmit), NTP, game state, and as the substrate for quic. For most backend engineers the operational facts about UDP are: it is stateless, so firewalls track it with timeouts (chapter 15); it is trivially spoofable, which is why it is used in amplification attacks and why your UDP services should never respond with more data than they receive to unauthenticated clients; and large UDP datagrams get fragmented at the IP layer, which is fragile across the Internet, so protocols keep them under ~1,200–1,400 bytes.

x: Each byte has a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects; the sender keeps unacknowledged data until acked and retransmits on a timeout or on receiving duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit). Selective acknowledgements (SACK) let the receiver report exactly which ranges arrived. A retransmission timeout stalls the stream; on a lossy link this is the "reliable connection that sometimes freezes for a second" you see on hotel Wi-Fi.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: The receiver advertises a window : how many more bytes it can buffer. The sender never has more than that in flight. A slow consumer (an application that does not read from the socket) shrinks the window to zero and the sender stops. This is backpressure at the transport layer, and it is why a slow client downloading a large response ties up a server worker in blocking servers.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: The sender also maintains a congestion window estimating how much the network can take. It starts small (slow start: roughly 10 segments, ~14 KB) and grows per round trip until loss or delay signals congestion, then shrinks. Algorithms differ (CUBIC is the Linux default; BBR models bandwidth and delay and is often better on lossy or long paths). Two practical results: - Small transfers are dominated by round trips, not bandwidth. The first 14 KB go in one RTT; a 100 KB response needs several RTTs of window growth. Keeping initial HTML and critical API responses small has outsized effect on perceived latency. - Loss on a long path collapses throughput. The bandwidth-delay product and loss rate set a ceiling; a 1% loss on a 100 ms path can limit a single TCP stream to a few Mbps regardless of link speed. Chapter 18.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: Either side sends FIN; the other acks and, when done, sends its own FIN, which is acked. The side that closed first waits in TIME-WAIT (2 × maximum segment lifetime, 60 s on Linux) so delayed packets from this connection cannot be mistaken for a new one using the same ports. A RST (reset) aborts a connection abruptly: sent when a segment arrives for a non-existent connection, when a process exits with unread data, or by firewalls and load balancers that want to drop you immediately. Clients see ECONNRESET / "connection reset by peer".

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: If a host crashes or a NAT entry expires, the other side may believe the connection is still established indefinitely; nothing in TCP detects an idle dead peer. TCP keep-alive sends probes after an idle period (Linux default 2 hours, far too long; set net.ipv4.tcp keepalive time=60 or enable at the socket level with shorter intervals). Databases, message brokers and load balancers each have their own idle timeouts; a connection pool must either keep connections warmer than the shortest timeout in the path or validate connections before use. This is the root cause behind a large share of "first request after idle fails" bugs.

Humans and configuration files use names; packets use addresses. Addresses change: load balancers scale, servers are replaced, providers migrate. DNS is the indirection layer that lets api.client.com keep working while everything behind it changes. It is also a globally distributed, heavily cached database with eventual consistency, and when it is wrong, everything is down while every server reports healthy. "It's always DNS" is a joke because it is so often true.

DNS names are read right to left: api.client.com. is the api label inside client inside com inside the root (the trailing dot, usually implicit). Each level is a zone served by authoritative name servers that hold the records for that zone and delegate sub-zones via NS records. - Root servers (13 named letters, hundreds of anycast instances) know the authoritative servers for every top-level domain. - TLD servers ( .com , .io , .de ) know the authoritative servers for each registered domain. - Your zone's authoritative servers (Route 53, Cloudflare, your registrar) hold the actual records.

A TTL is the number of seconds a resolver may cache a record. When you change a record, no message is sent to the world's resolvers; each one simply keeps the old answer until its copy expires. "Waiting for propagation" is waiting for caches to expire, and the wait is bounded by the old TTL, not the new one. Strategy for a planned change (migrating a load balancer, moving providers): 1. Days before: lower the TTL from 3600 to 60. Wait for the old TTL to expire everywhere (an hour). 2. Make the change. Within ~60 s, nearly all resolvers see it. Some misbehaving resolvers ignore TTLs; keep the old endpoint serving (or redirecting) for a day. 3. Afterwards: raise the TTL back if the record is stable, to reduce query volume and resolver dependence. Typical TTLs: 60–300 s for records that participate in failover or point at things that change (load balancers, blue/green switches); 3600–86400 s for stable records (MX, TXT, NS). Route 53 Alias records to AWS resources inherit the resource's TTL (60 s for ALBs) automatically. Negative caching: an NXDOMAIN ("does not exist") answer is cached too, for the SOA minimum TTL. Creating a record and testing it before it exists can poison your own resolver's cache for minutes; test with dig @authoritative-server first.

- Point names at load balancers via ALIAS/CNAME , never at instance IPs. ALB and NLB IPs change (NLBs can have static EIPs if you need them for allow-lists). - Apex domains ( client.com ) cannot use CNAME; use the provider's ALIAS feature or redirect the apex to www with a small static redirector. - Health-checked failover : Route 53 can return a secondary record when a health check fails (failover routing), route users to the nearest healthy region (latency routing), or split traffic by percentage (weighted routing) for gradual migrations. These all depend on TTLs; a 60 s TTL means up to 60 s of users still going to the dead endpoint, plus resolver misbehaviour. - Certificate validation : ACM and Let's Encrypt DNS-01 challenges work by asking you to publish a TXT or CNAME record; automation (Route 53 integration, cert-manager) makes this hands-free. - Internal DNS : inside a VPC, Route 53 private hosted zones let you name internal services ( db.internal.client.com ) without exposing records publicly; ECS Service Connect and Kubernetes CoreDNS provide service discovery names ( orders.svc.cluster.local ). - DNS is unauthenticated by default; a resolver can be fed forged answers (cache poisoning) and queries are visible to anyone on the path. DNSSEC signs zones so resolvers can verify answers (Route 53 supports signing; adoption is partial). DNS over HTTPS/TLS encrypts the client-to-resolver leg. - Dangling records are a common takeover vector: a CNAME pointing at a deprovisioned S3 bucket, Heroku app or Elastic Beanstalk environment can be claimed by an attacker who registers that resource name, giving them a page on your domain (subdomain takeover). Delete records when you delete resources; audit periodically. - CAA records limit which certificate authorities can issue for your domain. - Registrar security : the registrar account controls the NS records, and therefore everything. MFA, registry lock, and a shared ownership model (not a departed contractor's personal account) are essential. Domains expire; set auto-renew and calendar reminders, and make sure the payment card is not an individual's. - Email authentication records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) are DNS-based; without them your domain can be spoofed for phishing against your own client.

HTTP began as a way to fetch hypertext documents and became the universal application protocol: APIs, mobile backends, microservice calls, webhooks, streaming. Frameworks hide most of it, which is fine until a load balancer returns 502, a proxy strips a header, a client caches a response it should not have, or performance collapses because every request opens a new connection. The engineers who can read HTTP on the wire fix those in minutes.

A request is text: POST /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.client.com Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: 58 Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Accept: application/json User-Agent: client-app/2.4.0 {"customer_id":"c_123","items":[{"sku":"A1","qty":2}]} The request line gives the method, the path (plus query string) and the version. Headers are case-insensitive name-value pairs ending at a blank line. The body follows, with its length declared by Content-Length or sent in chunks with Transfer-Encoding: chunked . Host is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 and is how one IP serves many sites (virtual hosting) and how a load balancer picks a target group. A response mirrors it: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 142 Location: /api/v1/orders/o_789 Cache-Control: no-store X-Request-Id: 7f3a9c2e-... Date: Tue, 14 Mar 2026 10:21:07 GMT {"id":"o_789","status":"pending", ...}

Method Semantics Safe Idempotent Body --- --- --- --- --- GET Retrieve yes yes no HEAD GET without body yes yes no OPTIONS Capabilities; CORS preflight yes yes no POST Create or process; non-idempotent action no no yes PUT Replace the resource at this URL no yes yes PATCH Partial update no not by definition yes DELETE Remove no yes rarely "Safe" means no side effects (browsers and crawlers prefetch GETs; a GET that deletes something will be triggered by a link preview). "Idempotent" means repeating has the same result; proxies and clients may retry idempotent requests automatically after a network failure but must not retry POST. Part III chapters 2 and 3 build on this.

- 1xx informational: 100 Continue , 101 Switching Protocols (WebSocket upgrade). - 2xx success: 200 OK , 201 Created , 202 Accepted (queued for async processing), 204 No Content , 206 Partial Content . - 3xx redirection: 301 permanent (cached, method may change to GET), 302 / 303 temporary (use 303 See Other after POST), 304 Not Modified (conditional request hit), 307 / 308 temporary/permanent preserving method and body. - 4xx client errors: 400 Bad Request , 401 Unauthorized (actually "unauthenticated": missing or invalid credentials), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found , 405 Method Not Allowed , 409 Conflict , 410 Gone , 412 Precondition Failed , 413 Payload Too Large , 415 Unsupported Media Type , 422 Unprocessable Content (valid JSON, invalid semantics), 429 Too Many Requests . - 5xx server errors: 500 Internal Server Error , 501 Not Implemented , 502 Bad Gateway (proxy got an invalid response or connection failure from upstream), 503 Service Unavailable (overloaded or down; include Retry-After ), 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream too slow). The 502/503/504 distinction is diagnostic gold when a load balancer is involved: 502 means the backend connection failed or returned garbage (crashed process, wrong port, backend closed idle connection); 503 from an ALB means no healthy targets; 504 means the backend accepted but did not respond within the idle timeout (slow query, deadlock).

HTTP/1.0 opened a TCP connection per request. HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default ( Connection: keep-alive ), so many requests share one connection, amortising the handshake costs from chapter 6. But requests on one connection are sequential: the second cannot start until the first response completes (head-of-line blocking). Browsers open six parallel connections per host to compensate, and web performance folklore (domain sharding, sprite sheets, bundling) grew around that limit.

HTTP/2 (2015) keeps HTTP semantics (same methods, status codes, headers) and changes the wire format: - Binary framing instead of text. - Multiplexing : many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, interleaved; no application-level head-of-line blocking. One connection per origin. - Header compression (HPACK) : repeated headers (cookies, user agent) cost a few bytes. - Stream prioritisation and server push (push is now effectively dead; browsers removed it). - Browsers require TLS for HTTP/2 ( h2 ); the ALPN extension negotiates it during the TLS handshake. What it means for infrastructure: a client makes one TCP+TLS connection and sends everything over it. Load balancers typically terminate HTTP/2 from clients and speak HTTP/1.1 to backends (ALB does this by default; it can also use HTTP/2 or gRPC to targets). One remaining weakness: a single lost TCP segment stalls all streams until retransmitted, because TCP delivers in order.

HTTP/3 runs over quic instead of TCP: UDP-based, TLS 1.3 built in, independent streams so one loss does not block others, faster connection setup (1 RTT, 0 for resumption), and connection migration (your phone switches from Wi-Fi to cellular without dropping the connection). Browsers discover it via the Alt-Svc header or DNS HTTPS records and try it on UDP 443. For most backends, HTTP/3 is something the CDN or edge handles: CloudFront, Cloudflare and others terminate HTTP/3 from users and talk HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 to your origin. You get most of the benefit (faster, more resilient last mile) without changing your servers. Enabling it at the edge is usually a checkbox. Every packet between a user and your server crosses networks owned by strangers: coffee shop Wi-Fi, ISPs, exchange points, transit providers. Without protection, anyone on the path can read the traffic (passwords, tokens, personal data), modify it (inject scripts, change a payment amount) or impersonate the server. TLS solves all three for any TCP-based protocol: HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, and the same layer protects SMTP, PostgreSQL connections, gRPC and more.

1. Confidentiality : the application data is encrypted with keys only the two endpoints know. 2. Integrity : any modification in transit is detected and the connection fails. 3. Server authentication : the client verifies it is talking to the holder of a private key that a trusted certificate authority has bound to the hostname. Optionally, client authentication (mTLS) verifies the client too. What it does not do: hide that you are connecting, or to whom (IP addresses and, usually, the hostname via SNI are visible); protect data once decrypted at a load balancer or server; prevent attacks on the application itself; or help if the client is tricked into trusting a bad CA (corporate TLS interception, malware-installed roots).

TLS 1.2 (2008) is still widely supported and acceptable with modern cipher suites (ECDHE key exchange, AES-GCM or ChaCha20). Configure servers for TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only; use 1.3-only where every client is modern (service-to-service).

TLS encryption is easy; the hard part is knowing you are encrypting to the right party. A certificate is a third party's signed statement: "the holder of this public key controls api.client.com". The system of certificate authorities, trust stores, validation and revocation exists to make that statement trustworthy at Internet scale. Operationally, certificates are also time bombs: they expire, and expired certificates have taken down airlines, payment systems, cloud services and more.

An X.509 certificate contains: the subject (historically the Common Name; today the Subject Alternative Names extension lists the hostnames, and CN is ignored by browsers); the subject's public key ; the issuer (which CA signed it); validity dates (notBefore, notAfter); a serial number ; key usage and extended key usage (server auth, client auth); and the issuer's signature over all of it. openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text | head -40 # everything openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

h: Expiry: the outage you can schedule
x: Certificates expire at a known second. Yet expiry outages remain common because renewal depended on a person, or the automation broke silently (DNS credentials rotated, port 80 firewalled, a renewal cron removed during a server rebuild), or a certificate lived somewhere nobody remembered (an internal service, a webhook endpoint, a client-provided cert for mTLS). Defences, all of them: 1. Automate issuance and renewal everywhere; no manually installed public certificates. 2. Monitor expiry from the outside : a synthetic check that connects to every public endpoint and alerts at 21, 14 and 7 days remaining. Blackbox exporter (Prometheus), Route 53 health checks do not do this, so use a dedicated check or CloudWatch Synthetics canary. ACM emits DaysToExpiry metrics; alarm on them. 3. Monitor the renewal job , not just the certificate: a failed certbot renew should page before the certificate runs out. 4. Inventory : a list of every certificate, where it is installed, how it renews, who owns it. Include client-provided certificates and internal ones. 5. Test renewal when you build the system ( --dry-run ) and after any change to DNS, firewall or hosting. Public certificate maximum lifetimes are shrinking by industry decision (398 days today, with a published schedule toward 47 days by 2029). Manual renewal is becoming impossible by design; treat automation as mandatory now.

If a private key leaks, the certificate must be revoked. Mechanisms: CRLs (lists downloaded by clients, often stale), OCSP (clients ask the CA per certificate; privacy and availability problems), and OCSP stapling (the server fetches the OCSP response and includes it in the handshake; enable this). Browsers increasingly rely on their own aggregated revocation lists and short lifetimes rather than live checks. Practical conclusion: revocation is unreliable; short-lived certificates and prompt key rotation are the real control. If a key leaks, revoke and reissue and deploy immediately.

Inside a VPC or a client's network you may want TLS between services (ALB to backend, service to database, mTLS between services) with certificates for names that are not public ( orders.internal , 10.20.64.12 ). Options: - Self-signed per service : fine for ALB-to-backend re-encryption because the ALB does not validate; fragile anywhere a client does validate. - Private CA : a root (and intermediates) you control; clients trust it by installing the root. AWS Private CA (ACM PCA) does this as a managed service (notable monthly cost per CA); step-ca , HashiCorp Vault PKI, or cert-manager with a CA issuer in Kubernetes are common alternatives. Service meshes run their own. - Public certificates for internal names : possible if the names are under a public domain you control ( orders.internal.client.com ) and you use DNS-01; the certificates appear in public Certificate Transparency logs, revealing hostnames, which may or may not be acceptable. Operating a private CA means owning: root key protection (HSM or at least offline), intermediate rotation, distribution of the root to every client trust store (base images, config management, mobile devices), and revocation. Do not start one casually; do start one if you need mTLS between many services or encryption to backends that validate.

Every publicly trusted certificate is logged in public CT logs; browsers require proof of logging. Monitor CT for your domains (free services exist) to detect certificates issued without your knowledge, which indicates DNS compromise or a rogue CA. Set a caa DNS record so only your chosen CAs may issue.

HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone. Yet applications need to know that this request comes from the same user who logged in five minutes ago. Cookies are the browser-side mechanism for carrying a small piece of state, and sessions are the server-side pattern built on top. Because cookies are attached automatically by the browser, they are also the mechanism behind cross-site request forgery and a prime target for theft via XSS. Part IV chapters 4 and 9 cover the attacks in depth; this chapter establishes how the mechanism works.

A server sets a cookie with a response header; the browser stores it and attaches it to subsequent requests that match its scope. HTTP/1.1 200 OK Set-Cookie: __Host-session=8f3c1d...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=86400 GET /api/me HTTP/1.1 Host: app.client.com Cookie: __Host-session=8f3c1d... The browser decides whether to send a cookie based on the request's host (matching Domain), path , scheme (Secure), cross-site context (SameSite), and expiry . The server cannot see cookies that were not sent and cannot read cookies set by other sites.

Attribute Effect Recommendation --- --- --- Domain=client.com Sent to client.com and all subdomains Omit it. Without Domain, the cookie is host-only (sent only to the exact host that set it). Setting it widens exposure to every subdomain, including ones hosting user content or third-party tools. Path=/api Sent only for URLs under the path Use / . Path is not a security boundary (pages on the same origin can read each other's cookies via script). Expires / Max-Age Persistent cookie; otherwise a session cookie deleted when the browser closes (often not, with session restore) Set Max-Age explicitly for login sessions (hours to days) and rely on server-side expiry too. Secure Only sent over HTTPS Always. HttpOnly Not accessible to JavaScript ( document.cookie ) Always for session cookies. Blocks the most direct XSS theft path. SameSite=Strict Never sent on cross-site requests, even top-level navigation Strongest CSRF protection; breaks "arrive from an email link and be logged in". SameSite=Lax Sent on top-level GET navigations from other sites; not on cross-site POSTs, iframes, fetches Default choice. Good CSRF protection with normal UX. Modern browsers default to Lax when unspecified. SameSite=None Sent cross-site; requires Secure Only for cookies that must work in third-party contexts (embedded widgets, some SSO flows). Browsers cap cookies around 4 KB each and a few dozen per domain, and every cookie is sent with every request to matching hosts, including static assets. A 3 KB cookie on a page with 50 asset requests costs 150 KB of upload per page view. Keep cookies small (an opaque ID), and serve static assets from a cookieless domain or a CDN path that the cookie's scope does not cover.

The session pattern: the cookie holds an opaque, random session ID ; the server looks it up in a store (Redis, database, in-memory for a single process) to find the user and any state. # FastAPI sketch with Redis-backed sessions import secrets, json from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response, HTTPException SESSION_TTL = 60 * 60 * 12 async def create_session(redis, user_id: str) -> str: sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32) # 256 bits of randomness await redis.set(f"sess:{sid}", json.dumps({"uid": user_id, "created": now()}), ex=SESSION_TTL) return sid def set_session_cookie(resp: Response, sid: str): resp.set_cookie("__Host-sid", sid, max_age=SESSION_TTL, path="/", secure=True, httponly=True, samesite="lax") async def current_user(request: Request, redis): sid = request.cookies.get("__Host-sid") data = sid and await redis.get(f"sess:{sid}") if not data: raise HTTPException(401) await redis.expire(f"sess:{sid}", SESSION_TTL) # sliding expiry return json.loads(data)["uid"] Properties: revocable (delete the key and the user is logged out everywhere); small cookie ; server holds the state , so it needs a shared store once you have more than one server (sticky sessions are a fragile alternative). Requirements: IDs with at least 128 bits of entropy from a cryptographic RNG; rotate the ID on login (and on privilege change) to defeat session fixation; absolute and idle expiry; delete on logout; store minimal data.

The alternative is to put signed state in the cookie or in an Authorization: Bearer header: a jwt or an encrypted, signed cookie (Rails, Django's signed cookies). The server verifies the signature and trusts the contents without a lookup. Benefits: no shared store, easy horizontal scaling, usable across services. Costs: cannot be revoked before expiry without reintroducing a store (a denylist), tokens grow with claims, and any bug in signature verification is catastrophic. h: Cookies versus Authorization headers for SPAs
x: Single-page apps calling an API can store a token in JavaScript memory or localStorage and send it in the Authorization header, or rely on an HttpOnly cookie set by the API. Cookies are immune to theft via XSS (HttpOnly) but exposed to CSRF (mitigated by SameSite and tokens); header tokens are immune to CSRF but any XSS can steal them from storage. For a browser frontend on the same site as its API, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookies are the safer default. For third-party or mobile clients, bearer tokens in headers. Never store long-lived tokens in localStorage.

x: Application servers are good at running your code and bad at everything else: terminating TLS efficiently, serving static files, absorbing slow clients, enforcing request size limits, compressing responses, routing several applications on one host, and presenting a stable public surface while backends change. Nearly every production web deployment has at least one, whether it is Nginx on a VM, an ALB, a Kubernetes ingress controller, or a CDN.

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: A forward proxy acts for clients : the client is configured to send requests to the proxy, which fetches from the Internet on its behalf. You meet forward proxies in client environments where all outbound traffic must pass through one, and HTTPS PROXY environment variables suddenly matter. A reverse proxy acts for servers : clients connect to it believing it is the server; it forwards to one or more backends. x: - Buffering ( proxy buffering on ): Nginx reads the whole response from the app quickly and dribbles it out to a slow client, freeing the application worker. Without it, a few slow mobile clients can hold all your Gunicorn workers. The exception is streaming, where buffering breaks the feature. - client max body size : a 2 GB upload to an endpoint expecting 1 MB JSON would otherwise be read into the application's memory. - Timeouts : proxy read timeout is where 504s come from; set it with your slowest legitimate operation in mind, and move anything slower to a background job. - Upstream keepalive ( keepalive 32 plus Connection "" ): avoids a TCP handshake per request to the backend. - proxy next upstream : retries on another backend when one fails; only safe for idempotent requests, and Nginx by default does not retry non-idempotent methods after a partial send ( non idempotent flag changes that; leave it off).

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: The application sees the proxy's address as the TCP peer. The real client IP, scheme and host arrive in headers set by the proxy. Two rules: 1. The application trusts these headers only from its own proxies. If an attacker can reach the application directly (or if the proxy forwards client-supplied X-Forwarded-For unchanged), they can forge any IP, bypassing rate limits and poisoning audit logs. Bind the application to localhost or a private network; configure the framework's trusted-proxy list ( ProxyHeadersMiddleware / --forwarded-allow-ips in uvicorn, app.set('trust proxy', ...) in Express, SECURE PROXY SSL HEADER in Django) to the proxy's address only. 2. X-Forwarded-For is a list. client, proxy1, proxy2 . The rightmost entries were added by proxies you control; the leftmost is client-supplied and unverifiable unless your edge overwrites it. Take the entry just before your own proxies. For TCP proxies (NLB, HAProxy TCP mode) that cannot add HTTP headers, the PROXY protocol prepends a line with the original addresses to the connection; both sides must enable it.

h: The problem: one server is not enough
x: A single server has three limits. Capacity : CPU, memory, connections and bandwidth are finite; past a point, latency climbs and requests fail. Availability : when it reboots for a kernel patch, crashes, or its Availability Zone has a bad day, the service is down. Deployability : replacing the running process means downtime unless something else is serving meanwhile. You can buy a bigger server (vertical scaling): simple, no code changes, but it has a ceiling, gets expensive quickly, and still leaves one point of failure. Or you can run several identical servers (horizontal scaling) and put something in front that spreads traffic across them and avoids the broken ones. That something is a load balancer, and it quietly solves all three problems: capacity (add servers), availability (route around failures and AZ outages), and deployability (rolling updates behind a stable endpoint). Horizontal scaling requires the servers to be stateless (or share state through a database, cache or session store), which is why Part I chapter 14 and this part's cookie chapter insisted on it.

A Layer 4 load balancer works on TCP/UDP connections. It sees IP addresses and ports, picks a backend, and forwards packets (or proxies the connection) without reading the payload. Fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves end-to-end TLS. It cannot route by URL, inspect headers, or retry a failed HTTP request. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates the connection, parses HTTP, and makes decisions per request : route /api to one pool and / to another, by hostname, by header; add forwarding headers; terminate TLS; redirect HTTP to HTTPS; return fixed responses; integrate with a WAF; authenticate users (ALB can do OIDC); and multiplex many client connections into fewer backend connections. title AWS Network Load Balancer versus Application Load Balancer columns NLB (Layer 4) ALB (Layer 7) Protocols TCP, UDP, TLS HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets Routing by listener port only host, path, header, query, method, source IP passthrough, or terminate (TLS listener) without L7 features terminates; ACM certs; SNI with many certs per listener; optional re-encrypt to targets Client IP preservation yes, natively (source IP seen by target) or PROXY protocol via X-Forwarded-For Static IP / Elastic IP yes, one per AZ no (use DNS alias; or put an NLB in front via ALB-type target group) Performance millions of connections, ultra-low latency, handles spikes instantly high but warms up; very sudden spikes can see brief 5xx while scaling Health checks TCP, HTTP, HTTPS HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC with path and status co

The load balancer's health check is the single most important configuration you will set. It decides when a target gets traffic and when it is removed. Design the endpoint well: - Readiness, not liveness : /health/ready should return 200 only when the instance can serve real requests: configuration loaded, database reachable (a cheap SELECT 1 with a short timeout, or a cached dependency status), caches warm enough, not shutting down. Part XI chapter 5 discusses the tradeoff of including dependencies. - Cheap and fast : it runs every 10–30 seconds per target per load balancer node. Do not run heavy queries. - Fail during shutdown : return 503 as soon as SIGTERM arrives (Part I chapter 6). - Return 200 explicitly ; ALB defaults to expecting 200 but you can set 200-299 . Tune the parameters: interval 10 s, healthy threshold 2, unhealthy threshold 2 gives roughly 20 s to detect a dead target and 20 s to readmit a recovered one. The default 30 s interval with threshold 5 means 2.5 minutes of sending traffic to a dead target. Deregistration delay: 10–30 s for APIs (as long as your longest request), longer only for long-polling or uploads.

- Round robin : each new request to the next target. Fine when requests are similar. - Least outstanding requests (ALB option): send to the target with the fewest in-flight requests. Better when request costs vary or targets differ in capacity; the usual recommendation for APIs. - Weighted (target groups with weights): canary deployments, blue-green traffic shifting. - Flow hash (NLB): 5-tuple hash so a connection always goes to the same target; inherent to L4. - Least connections / IP hash / consistent hashing : common in Nginx and HAProxy; consistent hashing matters for cache tiers where you want the same key on the same node.

Stickiness routes the same client to the same target, via a load-balancer cookie (ALB AWSALB ) or an application cookie. It exists for applications that keep session state in process memory. Costs: uneven load, loss of sessions on deploy or scale-in, and complexity. Prefer shared session stores (chapter 11) and leave stickiness off; enable it only as a bridge for legacy applications you cannot change, and document it as debt.

The ALB terminates TLS with ACM certificates: one per listener plus additional certificates served by SNI, or a wildcard. Enable HTTP→HTTPS redirect on the :80 listener as a redirect action. Choose a modern security policy. To targets, speak HTTP on the private network, or HTTPS if policy demands (the ALB will not validate the target's certificate name, so self-signed works). Chapter 9's diagram covers the options.

The ALB keeps connections to targets alive and reuses them. Two timeouts matter: the ALB idle timeout (default 60 s) applies to client and target connections; your target's keep-alive timeout must be longer (e.g. 120 s) or you get intermittent 502s. For long-running requests (large uploads, slow reports) raise the idle timeout, but anything over a minute should become asynchronous. The ALB generates X-Forwarded-For , X-Forwarded-Proto , X-Forwarded-Port , and X-Amzn-Trace-Id (a request ID you should log). Enable access logs to S3; they include target processing time and the status code the target returned versus what the ALB returned, which separates "app is slow" from "ALB is slow".

HTTP's request-response model does not fit everything. A chat app needs the server to push messages the instant they arrive; a dashboard wants live metrics; a long-running job needs to report progress; services calling each other thousands of times a second want less overhead than JSON over HTTP/1.1. Several protocols extend or replace plain HTTP for these cases, and each one has infrastructure consequences: connection counts, proxy configuration, load balancer timeouts and stateful servers.

A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade ; the server replies 101 Switching Protocols , and from then on the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames in both directions until either side closes. Messages are framed (text or binary) with no HTTP semantics; you design the message protocol. // Server (Node, ws library) with heartbeat to detect dead clients import { WebSocketServer } from 'ws'; const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server, path: '/ws' }); wss.on('connection', (ws, req) => { const user = authenticate(req); // cookie or token in query/first message; reject early if (!user) return ws.close(4401, 'unauthorized'); ws.isAlive = true; ws.on('pong', () => { ws.isAlive = true; }); ws.on('message', (buf) => handle(user, JSON.parse(buf))); }); setInterval(() => wss.clients.forEach((ws) => { // every 30 s: terminate silent clients, ping the rest if (!ws.isAlive) return ws.terminate(); ws.isAlive = false; ws.ping(); }), 30_000); Infrastructure requirements: the proxy must forward the Upgrade headers ( proxy set header Upgrade $http upgrade; Connection "upgrade" in Nginx; ALB supports WebSockets natively on HTTP/HTTPS listeners); idle timeouts must exceed your ping interval; and each connection consumes a file descriptor and some memory on a specific server for its lifetime.

Persistent connections make servers stateful: user A is connected to server 1; a message for A arriving at server 2 must be routed to server 1. The standard solution is a pub/sub backplane : every server subscribes to a channel (Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams, SNS/SQS, Kafka); a message for A is published; the server holding A's connection delivers it. Connection counts per server are bounded by memory and file descriptors (tens of thousands per modest instance), so capacity planning is "connections per instance × instances", and deployments must handle mass reconnection (clients reconnect with randomised backoff, or storms follow). Managed alternatives: API Gateway WebSocket APIs, AppSync, Pusher, Ably. Authentication: browsers cannot set custom headers on WebSocket handshakes, so authenticate via the session cookie (SameSite rules apply), a short-lived token in the first message, or a one-time ticket in the URL (never a long-lived token in the URL; it lands in logs). Check Origin on the handshake to prevent cross-site WebSocket hijacking.

gRPC is an RPC framework: you define services and messages in Protocol Buffers, generate typed clients and servers for many languages, and calls travel as HTTP/2 streams with binary payloads. It supports unary calls and client-, server- and bidirectional streaming, deadlines propagated across hops, and rich status codes. syntax = "proto3"; service Orders { rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order); rpc WatchOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (stream OrderEvent); // server streaming } message GetOrderRequest { string id = 1; } message Order { string id = 1; string status = 2; repeated LineItem items = 3; } Why teams use it internally: strict contracts with generated code, small fast messages, streaming, deadlines and cancellation built in. Why not to browsers: browsers cannot speak raw gRPC (no control over HTTP/2 framing); grpc-web requires a proxy (Envoy) and loses some streaming modes. Why not for public APIs: tooling and debuggability ( curl cannot easily call it; use grpcurl ), and partners expect REST/JSON. Infrastructure: gRPC needs HTTP/2 end to end . An ALB supports gRPC target groups (protocol version gRPC) with gRPC-aware health checks and routing on service/method paths; Nginx proxies gRPC with grpc pass ; a plain L7 proxy that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 breaks it. Because one HTTP/2 connection carries many calls, L4 load balancing (NLB, Kubernetes Service) pins all of a client's calls to one backend; use an L7 balancer or client-side load balancing for even distribu

- Reconnection : clients must reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and resume from a cursor ( Last-Event-ID , a sequence number) so no events are lost or duplicated. Servers must tolerate reconnect storms after a deploy. - Backpressure : a slow consumer must not make the server buffer unboundedly. Bound per-connection queues; drop or coalesce low-value updates (the latest metric value supersedes old ones); close abusive connections. - Idle and dead connections : TCP will not tell you a client vanished. Use protocol-level pings and close on missed pongs. - Observability : track active connections per instance, messages per second, send-queue depth, reconnect rate. These are your capacity and health signals. - Deploys : a rolling deploy disconnects every client on the old instances. Drain gracefully (send a "reconnect" message, close with a code), and stagger instance replacement so reconnects spread out. - Authorization per message , not just per connection: a connection opened by user A must not be able to subscribe to user B's channel because the server forgot to check on subscribe.

A server offers services on ports. Every open port reachable from an untrusted network is an attack surface: a database with a weak password, an admin interface, a debug endpoint, SSH exposed to password guessing. Firewalls restrict which sources can reach which ports, turning "everything is reachable unless the application defends itself" into "nothing is reachable unless explicitly allowed". They are the first and cheapest layer of defense in depth, and most of the catastrophic breaches of exposed databases needed only a firewall rule to prevent.

A stateless filter evaluates each packet alone against rules on source/destination address, protocol and port. To allow a TCP connection it needs two rules: inbound to the server port, and outbound from the server port back to the client's ephemeral ports (1024–65535), because it does not know the reply belongs to an existing connection. AWS Network ACLs are stateless. A stateful filter tracks connections. When an inbound packet is allowed and a connection is established, the return traffic is allowed automatically. One rule ("allow inbound 443 from anywhere") suffices; replies just work. AWS security groups, Linux nftables / iptables with conntrack, ufw , and nearly all modern firewalls are stateful. Stateful filters hold a connection table with timeouts (minutes for established TCP, seconds for UDP). Idle connections dropped from the table die silently, the same phenomenon as NAT in chapter 4; keep-alives are the cure.

The correct posture: deny everything, then allow the minimum . Inbound: only the ports the public needs (443, maybe 80 for redirects) from everywhere; administrative access (SSH) from specific addresses or via a bastion/VPN; internal services only from the components that use them. Outbound: ideally restricted too (a compromised server that cannot reach the Internet cannot download tools or exfiltrate data), though outbound allow-lists are operationally demanding and most teams start with outbound open and tighten for sensitive tiers.

Outbound filtering is where mature environments differentiate themselves. Options in increasing strictness: security group outbound rules (by port/destination SG), route tables that keep private subnets off the Internet entirely (with VPC endpoints for AWS services), a NAT instance or AWS Network Firewall with domain allow-lists, or an explicit forward proxy that only permits known hosts. For client systems handling sensitive data, "the database tier cannot reach the Internet" is both a strong control and a simple one to implement with route tables and security groups.

A waf inspects HTTP requests after TLS termination and blocks patterns: SQL injection and XSS signatures, known bad bots, request floods (rate-based rules), geographic restrictions, and custom rules (block requests without a required header, or to admin paths from outside an IP set). AWS WAF attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway and AppSync; managed rule groups cover the common cases. Treat WAF as a shield that buys time and reduces noise, not as security: it can be bypassed by encoding tricks, it produces false positives (legitimate payloads containing SQL keywords), and it never fixes the underlying vulnerability. Start in count mode, review what would be blocked, then enforce.

The signature of a firewall is a timeout : packets dropped silently. (Some firewalls reject with RST or ICMP, giving "connection refused" or "unreachable" quickly, which is kinder to debuggers.) # From the client side nc -vz -w 3 10.20.128.10 5432 # times out → filtered somewhere; refused → reachable, nothing listening # AWS: Reachability Analyzer traces a path and names the blocking SG/NACL/route aws ec2 create-network-insights-path --source eni-app --destination eni-db --destination-port 5432 --protocol tcp # VPC Flow Logs show REJECT records with the interface and ports # On the host: are packets arriving at all? (if yes, the host firewall or the app is the problem) sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp port 5432 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' sudo nft list ruleset | grep -n 5432; sudo ufw status sudo journalctl -k | grep 'nft-drop' # logged drops Method: confirm the destination is listening ( ss -ltn on the target); confirm packets reach the target ( tcpdump there); if not, walk outward: host firewall, security group of the target, NACL of the target subnet, route tables, security group outbound of the source, NACL of the source subnet. Reachability Analyzer does this walk for you in AWS.

- Explain what a VPN provides and the difference between site-to-site, client and mesh VPNs. - Choose between a bastion host, SSM Session Manager, a client VPN and a zero-trust access proxy for administrative access. - Connect a VPC privately to a client's network or to other VPCs: VPN, Direct Connect, peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink. - Avoid the mistakes that make private connectivity either insecure or unmaintainable. ::: Chapters 4, 9 and 15. :::

Your database lives in a private subnet with no public address, as it should. Now a developer needs to run a query, a client's on-premises system needs to call your API without exposing it to the Internet, two VPCs need to talk, and an auditor asks how administrators reach production. "Private connectivity" is the set of mechanisms for reaching things that are deliberately unreachable from the public Internet, and each mechanism trades security, cost and convenience differently.

A Virtual Private Network creates an encrypted tunnel between two endpoints over an untrusted network, and makes remote networks appear local by routing traffic for their address ranges through the tunnel. Packets to 10.20.128.10 on your laptop are encrypted, sent to the VPN gateway's public address, decrypted there and forwarded into the VPC. Authentication is by certificates, pre-shared keys or an identity provider. Protocols: IPsec (the standard for site-to-site between routers and cloud gateways; complex but universal), WireGuard (modern, minimal, fast, in the Linux kernel; the basis of Tailscale and many self-hosted setups), OpenVPN (older, flexible, widely supported including AWS Client VPN), and TLS-based vendor VPNs.

Connects two networks: a client's office or data centre to your VPC. AWS Site-to-Site VPN pairs a Virtual Private Gateway (or Transit Gateway) with the client's firewall as a "customer gateway" over two IPsec tunnels for redundancy. Routing is static or via BGP. Throughput per tunnel is limited (1.25 Gbps). Address ranges must not overlap, which is why chapter 3 insisted on planning CIDRs.

Connects individual users' devices. AWS Client VPN (OpenVPN-based, authenticates with certificates, Active Directory or SAML) or self-hosted WireGuard/OpenVPN on a small instance. Users get a tunnel into the VPC for administrative access. Costs: per-endpoint-hour plus per-connection-hour for AWS Client VPN; a self-hosted WireGuard instance costs a few dollars a month but is yours to patch.

Tailscale, ZeroTier, Cloudflare WARP/Access and similar build an identity-based mesh where every device authenticates to a control plane and connects peer-to-peer over WireGuard, with access control lists per user and service. They remove the "once inside, everything is reachable" weakness of classic VPNs and are quick to set up; the trade is dependency on a third party's control plane for your access path.

A direct, non-transitive connection between two VPCs (same or different accounts/regions). Traffic stays on the AWS network. Each VPC adds routes for the other's CIDR; security groups can reference peered groups in the same region. Non-transitive means A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C. Fine for a handful of VPCs; a mess beyond that.

A regional hub that VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect attach to, with route tables controlling who can reach whom. Transitive, scalable, auditable; hourly cost per attachment plus per-GB. The standard for organisations with many VPCs or a hybrid network.

A dedicated physical link from a client's data centre to AWS via a partner location. Consistent latency and bandwidth (1–100 Gbps), traffic off the public Internet, lower data-transfer prices for heavy volumes; weeks to provision and significant fixed cost. Usually paired with a VPN as backup. Relevant when a client has serious on-premises systems; an FDE rarely provisions it but often works within it.

- A private network is not a trusted network. Encrypt in transit (TLS) over VPNs and peering too; authenticate every request. Private links reduce exposure; they do not replace application security. This is the core of zero trust. - Least privilege at the network layer still applies : a VPN user should reach the tools they need, not the whole VPC. Use security groups referencing the VPN's address pool narrowly, and client VPN authorization rules. - Audit every administrative session : SSM logs by default; bastions and VPNs need deliberate logging. - Avoid split-brain address plans : overlapping CIDRs force NAT hacks that nobody understands a year later. - Rotate and revoke : VPN certificates and WireGuard keys for people who leave; SSM access via IAM groups tied to the identity provider so offboarding is automatic. - Do not expose internal admin tools publicly behind "only we know the URL". - Explain how a CDN serves content from the edge and what it can and cannot cache. - Design cache keys, TTLs, invalidation and origin configuration so that users get fast responses and never someone else's data. - Use CloudFront (or an equivalent) in front of static sites, APIs and media correctly. - Recognise when a CDN is unnecessary and when it is essential. ::: Chapters 1, 8 and 18 (latency) are closely related; read chapter 8 first. :::

Physics sets a floor on latency: a user in Sydney fetching from a server in Virginia waits 200 ms per round trip, and a page needs several. Meanwhile your origin serves the same static files millions of times, and a traffic spike or attack hits it directly. A Content Delivery Network places servers in hundreds of cities, answers users from the nearest one, caches what can be cached, absorbs floods, and terminates TLS close to the user so even uncacheable API calls get faster handshakes. In exchange you take on a new class of bugs: cache poisoning, stale content, and the infamous "user A sees user B's account page".

- Fingerprinted static assets ( app.3f9a1c.js , logo.8bd2.png ): cache forever ( max-age=31536000, immutable ). The filename changes when content changes, so invalidation is never needed. Every modern bundler does this. - HTML shells and unfingerprinted files ( /index.html ): short TTL (seconds to minutes) or no-cache with ETag revalidation, so deploys take effect quickly. - Public API responses (product catalogue, public feeds): short s-maxage with stale-while-revalidate , keyed carefully on query parameters. - Media and downloads : long TTLs; range requests supported. - Personal or authenticated responses : never at a shared cache. Cache-Control: private, no-store , and configure the CDN behaviour for those paths to bypass caching entirely regardless of headers.

h: Cache keys and the "wrong user's data" disaster
x: The cache key decides which requests share a cached response. Too narrow (every header included) and nothing is ever a hit; too broad and responses leak between users. The classic incident: a CDN configured to cache based on URL only, an API endpoint /api/account that varies by session cookie, and a missing no-store . User A's account JSON is cached and served to users B through Z for the TTL. Defences, all of them: 1. Mark personal responses Cache-Control: private, no-store at the application. 2. Configure CDN behaviours per path: /api/ with caching disabled (CloudFront "CachingDisabled" policy) and all headers, cookies and query strings forwarded. 3. Include the relevant varying inputs in the cache key for anything that is cached and varies ( Vary: Accept-Encoding ; for per-language content, the Accept-Language header or a path prefix). Never include cookies in the cache key for public content (it destroys the hit rate); never cache content that depends on cookies. 4. Test it: fetch an authenticated endpoint as user A, then as user B, through the CDN, and compare; check the X-Cache / Age response headers to confirm misses.

Caches expire by TTL. To change content before expiry you invalidate (CloudFront: create an invalidation for paths; first 1,000 paths per month free, then per path) or purge (Cloudflare, Fastly: fast and cheap, often tag-based). t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: "The API is slow" is the most common complaint and the least specific. Slowness has at least four distinct physical causes with different remedies, and most engineers reach for the wrong one: they optimise database queries when the user is 200 ms away, or buy bandwidth when the problem is round trips. This chapter gives you the vocabulary and the arithmetic to diagnose performance before touching code.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: - Latency : time for a unit of data to travel from source to destination (one-way), or the time for a request to get a response (round-trip time, RTT). Measured in milliseconds. Set by distance, hops and queueing. - Bandwidth : the capacity of a link, in bits per second. A 1 Gbps link can carry a gigabit per second if the protocol can use it. - Throughput : what you actually achieve: bytes per second transferred, or requests per second served. Always at or below bandwidth; often far below, limited by latency, loss and protocol behaviour. - Jitter : variation in latency. Matters for real-time media; a buffer absorbs it at the cost of added latency. - Packet loss : fraction of packets that do not arrive. Even 0.1% has outsized effects on TCP throughput over long paths. The intuition: bandwidth is how wide the pipe is; latency is how long the pipe is; throughput is how much water you actually move, which depends on both and on how the protocol behaves.

h: Why round trips dominate small requests
x: A new HTTPS request costs: DNS (0–1 RTT), TCP handshake (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT), request and first byte (1 RTT), plus server processing. For a Sydney user hitting Virginia (200 ms RTT): 600–800 ms before the server has even done any work, for a response that takes 5 ms to compute. With a warm, reused connection it is 200 ms plus 5. This is why: - Connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2, connection pools) is the first performance tool. - Fewer, larger requests beat many small ones over high-latency links (and HTTP/2 multiplexing mitigates the many-small-requests cost). - Sequential dependent calls are latency multipliers : a page that loads HTML, then JS, then calls an API that calls another service, each dependent on the last, pays an RTT per step. Parallelise what can be parallel. - Chatty service-to-service calls across regions are architectural errors; keep tightly coupled services in the same region (ideally same AZ for the hottest paths, accepting the availability trade).

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
h: Why throughput falls short of bandwidth
x: TCP's congestion window limits how much data is in flight per RTT. Maximum throughput of one connection ≈ window ÷ RTT. With a 64 KB window and 100 ms RTT: 640 KB/s ≈ 5 Mbps, regardless of a 10 Gbps link. Modern stacks scale windows into megabytes, but loss resets growth. The Mathis formula gives the loss-limited ceiling: throughput ≈ (MSS ÷ RTT) × (1.22 ÷ √loss). At 100 ms RTT, 1,460-byte segments and 1% loss, that is about 1.4 Mbps per connection. Hence: - Long-distance, lossy paths need parallel connections or BBR congestion control to fill a link; or, better, move the data closer (CDN, regional buckets, S3 Transfer Acceleration). - Inside a region, loss is near zero and RTT is ~1 ms, so throughput approaches the link rate; EC2 instance bandwidth limits (which scale with instance size and are burstable on small types) become the ceiling. - Bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth × RTT) is the buffer size needed to keep a link full: 1 Gbps × 100 ms = 12.5 MB. Kernel defaults handle this now; very fast long links may still need tuning ( net.ipv4.tcp rmem/wmem ).

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: Time to transmit a payload = size ÷ bandwidth, added to latency. On a 10 Mbps mobile link, a 2 MB JavaScript bundle costs 1.6 s of pure transmission; on 100 ms RTT with slow start it costs several more RTTs. Compression (gzip/Brotli for text), smaller payloads (pagination, field selection, binary formats), image optimisation and code splitting attack this term. For APIs, a 1 MB JSON response that the client discards 90% of is a design problem visible in every metric.
